title: Theogony
creator: hesiod
location: Boeotia, Greece; survives in medieval Byzantine manuscripts
note: The Greek account of the origins of the cosmos and the generations of the gods, culminating in the reign of Zeus.
description: The Theogony, about a thousand lines of hexameter verse, opens with Hesiod's encounter with the Muses on Mount Helicon and then tells how the world came to be: first Chaos, then Earth (Gaia), Tartarus and Eros, followed by the generations of gods born from Earth and Sky (Ouranos). It narrates the castration of Ouranos by his son Kronos, Kronos's swallowing of his children, and the victory of Zeus and the Olympians over the Titans, along with the story of Prometheus and the first woman. Scholars have noted close parallels with Near Eastern succession myths, such as the Hittite Kumarbi cycle and the Babylonian Enuma Elish, suggesting cultural contact. The poem became the standard Greek genealogy of the gods, used by later poets, mythographers and philosophers, and remains the starting point for the study of Greek mythology.
image_caption: The Theogony in a medieval Greek manuscript, Biblioteca Marciana, Venice (Gr. 464)

title: Works and Days
creator: hesiod
note: A farmer's poem of advice to Hesiod's brother, weaving together myths, moral teaching, the agricultural calendar and lucky and unlucky days.
description: Works and Days is addressed to Hesiod's brother Perses, who had apparently cheated him over their inheritance with the help of corrupt judges. Hesiod urges him to honest labour and justice, which Zeus protects. Along the way he tells the myth of Pandora, who released evils into the world, and the myth of the five ages of humankind, from the golden race to the present iron age. The second half gives practical instruction on farming and sailing through the seasons, ending with a list of days of the month favourable or unfavourable for various tasks. The poem is a key witness to the everyday piety of archaic Greece, in which the gods are bound up with work, weather and fairness, and it was the model for later didactic poetry such as Virgil's Georgics.

title: Homeric Hymn to Demeter
creator: homeric-hymn-poets
location: Rediscovered in a manuscript in Moscow, 1777; now in Leiden University Library
note: The myth of Persephone's abduction and Demeter's grief, telling the origin of the Eleusinian Mysteries.
description: This hymn of nearly five hundred lines tells how Hades, with Zeus's consent, seized Persephone, daughter of the grain goddess Demeter, and carried her to the underworld. Demeter wanders the earth in mourning, disguised as an old woman, and takes service as a nurse in the royal house of Eleusis. When her divinity is revealed she orders a temple built there and withholds the growth of crops until Zeus forces Hades to return Persephone. Because Persephone has eaten a pomegranate seed she must spend part of each year below. Before returning to Olympus, Demeter teaches the Eleusinians her secret rites, which bring blessing to initiates in this life and the next. The Eleusinian Mysteries were celebrated for about a thousand years until they were suppressed at the end of the 4th century AD, and the hymn is one of the principal sources for them, although it guards their secrets.
image_caption: The Great Eleusinian Relief: Demeter, Persephone and the youth Triptolemus, c. 440–430 BC (National Archaeological Museum, Athens)

title: Torah (Five Books of Moses)
creator: hebrew-bible-authors
location: Ancient Israel and Babylon; read in synagogues from handwritten scrolls
note: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy: the story from creation to the death of Moses, and the laws of the covenant at Sinai.
description: The Torah, also called the Pentateuch, is the first and most sacred division of the Hebrew Bible. It runs from the creation of the world and the stories of Adam and Eve, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph, through the enslavement of the Israelites in Egypt, the Exodus led by Moses and the giving of the law at Mount Sinai, to the wanderings in the wilderness and Moses's death on the threshold of the promised land. Woven through the narrative are the Ten Commandments and extensive laws on worship, purity, justice and social life. Jewish and Christian tradition held Moses to be its author. From the 19th century the 'documentary hypothesis' proposed that it combined four main sources, often labelled J, E, D and P, written in different periods; scholars today continue to debate the number, nature and dating of its sources, but most agree it reached its final form around the 5th century BC, during or after the Babylonian exile. Handwritten on parchment scrolls by trained scribes, the Torah is read in a yearly cycle in synagogues and is the foundation of Jewish law and life.
image_caption: A handwritten Torah scroll (National Library of Belarus)

title: Psalms
creator: hebrew-bible-authors
note: One hundred and fifty songs of praise, lament, thanksgiving and wisdom, the prayer book of Judaism and Christianity.
description: The Book of Psalms collects 150 poems, divided into five books, many of them headed with the names of David, Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon or Moses. Tradition attributed most of them to King David. Modern scholars see the Psalms as having been composed over several centuries, some perhaps for worship in the First Temple and others in the exile and after, and compiled into the present collection in the Second Temple period, though the dating of individual psalms is much debated. They include hymns of praise, laments of individuals and of the people, royal psalms, songs of pilgrimage and meditations on the law. Their parallelism and imagery, from the shepherd of Psalm 23 to the exiles weeping by the rivers of Babylon in Psalm 137, have made them the most used part of the Bible in prayer. They are central to Jewish liturgy and to the daily offices of Christian monks, and have been set to music, versified and translated countless times.
image_caption: The Great Psalms Scroll (11Q5) from Qumran Cave 11

title: Book of Isaiah
creator: hebrew-bible-authors
note: Prophecies of judgement and comfort, from the Jerusalem prophet of the 8th century BC and, most scholars think, later disciples.
description: Isaiah is the first and longest of the major prophetic books. Its earliest layers are associated with Isaiah son of Amoz, who prophesied in Jerusalem during the Assyrian crisis of the late 8th century BC, warning kings of Judah and calling for justice and trust in God. Since the late 18th century most scholars have held that chapters 40–55, which speak of Cyrus of Persia and the return from Babylonian exile, come from an anonymous prophet of the 6th century often called Second Isaiah, and that chapters 56–66 are later still, while traditional readers regard the whole book as the work of the one prophet. Its visions of the holy God enthroned in the temple, of swords beaten into ploughshares and of the suffering servant made it hugely influential: it is the prophetic book most cited in the New Testament, and Christians read many passages as foretelling Christ. A complete scroll of Isaiah is among the Dead Sea Scrolls.
image_caption: Isaiah 53 in the Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, 2nd century BC

title: Book of Job
creator: hebrew-bible-authors
note: A righteous man loses everything and argues with his friends and with God about why the innocent suffer.
description: The Book of Job sets a long poetic debate inside a prose folk tale. In the frame story God allows 'the Satan', a heavenly accuser, to test the blameless Job by destroying his wealth, his children and his health. In the poetry Job curses the day of his birth, and three friends insist his suffering must be punishment for sin, which he denies, demanding a hearing from God. God finally answers from the whirlwind with a series of questions about the wonders of creation, without explaining Job's suffering, and in the prose ending restores his fortunes. Scholars usually date the book to the exilic or post-exilic period, while acknowledging that its language makes dating difficult. Its bold questioning of easy answers about suffering has fascinated theologians, philosophers and writers from Gregory the Great to Kierkegaard, Blake and modern novelists.
image_caption: Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 3522, a 1st-century fragment of Job in Greek

title: Song of Songs
creator: hebrew-bible-authors
note: A sequence of erotic love poems between a woman and a man, read allegorically by Jews and Christians as the love between God and his people or the soul.
description: The Song of Songs, also called the Song of Solomon or Canticles, is a collection of lyrical poems in which two lovers, the woman's voice especially prominent, speak of desire, longing, separation and union, with rich imagery of gardens, vineyards, spices and animals. God is not named in it. Its heading attributes it to Solomon; scholars propose dates from the monarchy to the Hellenistic period, often favouring a late date on linguistic grounds. Rabbi Akiva is said to have called it the 'holy of holies' among the scriptures, and Jewish tradition read it as an allegory of the love between God and Israel; it is read at Passover. Christian commentators, from Origen to Bernard of Clairvaux, interpreted it as the love of Christ for the church or for the individual soul, and it became a principal source of mystical language. Modern readers have also valued it as celebration of human love.
image_file: Gustave Moreau - Song of Songs (Cantique des Cantiques) - Google Art Project.jpg
image_caption: Gustave Moreau, The Song of Songs, 1853

title: Book of Daniel
creator: hebrew-bible-authors
year: c. 167–164 BC (set in the 6th century BC)
note: Tales of a Jewish sage at the court of Babylon and visions of world empires and the coming kingdom of God.
description: The first half of Daniel tells stories of Daniel and his companions, Jewish exiles at the courts of Babylon and Persia who stay faithful to God: the fiery furnace, the writing on the wall at Belshazzar's feast, and Daniel in the lions' den. The second half records visions of four beasts representing successive empires, of 'one like a son of man' coming with the clouds of heaven, and of a time of persecution followed by resurrection of the dead. Traditional readers take the book as written by Daniel in the 6th century BC. Most modern scholars date its final form to the persecution of the Jews by the Seleucid king Antiochus IV around 167–164 BC, since its visions describe those events in detail, while the court tales may be older. Daniel is the chief example of apocalyptic literature in the Hebrew Bible and deeply influenced the New Testament, Revelation and later speculation about the end of the world.
image_caption: A fragment of Daniel among the Dead Sea Scrolls

title: Book of Ruth
creator: hebrew-bible-authors
year: c. 6th–4th century BC (set in the time of the Judges)
note: A short story of loyalty in which a Moabite widow follows her mother-in-law to Bethlehem and becomes the great-grandmother of King David.
description: Set in the period of the Judges, Ruth tells how Naomi, widowed and bereaved of her sons in Moab, returns to Bethlehem with her Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth, who refuses to leave her, saying that Naomi's people will be her people and Naomi's God her God. Gleaning in the fields of Naomi's kinsman Boaz, Ruth wins his protection, and he marries her according to the custom of the kinsman-redeemer. Their son Obed is the grandfather of David. Scholars debate its date, from the monarchy to the post-exilic period; some read it as a gentle response to post-exilic hostility to foreign wives. In Jewish tradition Ruth is read at the festival of Shavuot and is the model of a convert; in the Christian Gospel of Matthew she appears in the genealogy of Jesus.
image_caption: William Blake, Naomi entreating Ruth and Orpah to return to the land of Moab, 1795

title: Book of Ecclesiastes (Qoheleth)
creator: hebrew-bible-authors
note: The reflections of 'the Teacher' on the vanity of human striving and the enjoyment of life as God's gift.
description: Ecclesiastes presents the words of Qoheleth, 'the one who assembles', identified as a son of David and king in Jerusalem, hence the traditional attribution to Solomon. Its refrain, often translated 'vanity of vanities, all is vanity' (hevel, literally 'breath' or 'vapour'), introduces meditations on the limits of wisdom, the injustice of the world, the certainty of death and the cyclical nature of time, with the famous poem 'to every thing there is a season'. Against this background it repeatedly counsels enjoyment of food, work and love as gifts of God, and ends with an epilogue urging the fear of God. Most scholars date it, on linguistic grounds, to the Persian or early Hellenistic period. Its scepticism made its inclusion in the canon debated among the rabbis, and it has appealed to readers from Montaigne to modern existentialists.
image_file: Dead Sea Scroll 109, Qohelet or Ecclesiastes, from Qumran Cave 4. The Jordan Museum, Amman.jpg
image_caption: Fragment of Ecclesiastes from Qumran Cave 4 (The Jordan Museum, Amman)

title: The Pilgrim's Progress
creator: bunyan
note: Bunyan's dream allegory of Christian's journey from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City.
description: Bunyan began The Pilgrim's Progress during his imprisonment in Bedford gaol. The narrator dreams of a man called Christian, burdened with sin, who leaves the City of Destruction for the Celestial City. On the way he loses his burden at the cross, passes through the Slough of Despond, Vanity Fair, where his companion Faithful is martyred, and Doubting Castle, kept by Giant Despair, and meets characters such as Evangelist, Mr Worldly Wiseman and Hopeful, before crossing the river of death. The second part, of 1684, follows his wife Christiana and their children. Written in plain, vivid prose drawing on the Bible and popular storytelling, it was an immediate success and has been translated into some two hundred languages, carried worldwide by missionaries. It has been called one of the first English novels and influenced writers from Defoe to Thackeray and Louisa May Alcott.
image_caption: Title page of the first edition, 1678

title: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners
creator: bunyan
note: Bunyan's account of his years of spiritual torment and conversion, a classic of Puritan autobiography.
description: Written in prison and published in 1666, Grace Abounding tells Bunyan's story as a spiritual drama: a youth of swearing and games, his marriage and first stirrings of piety, and then years of agonising doubt in which he feared he had committed the unforgivable sin, tormented by verses of scripture that seemed to condemn or save him by turns. He finally finds assurance in Christ, and then describes his call to preach and his imprisonment. It is one of the most psychologically intense religious autobiographies in English and a key text for understanding Puritan experience of conversion.
image_caption: Title page of Grace Abounding

title: Pia Desideria
creator: spener
note: Spener's 'Heartfelt Desires' for the reform of the Lutheran church, the founding manifesto of Pietism.
description: Pia Desideria was first published as a preface to a new edition of the sermons of Johann Arndt, author of True Christianity, and soon issued separately. Spener describes the corruption of the church, among rulers, clergy and people, and expresses hope for better times. He proposes six reforms: more extensive use of scripture, including in small groups; the exercise of the priesthood of all believers; an emphasis on practical Christian life over knowledge; charity in religious controversy; reform of theological education to cultivate piety; and preaching aimed at edification rather than display. The programme gave rise to Pietism in Germany and influenced the Moravians and Methodists.

title: Shivhei ha-Besht (In Praise of the Baal Shem Tov)
creator: baal-shem-tov
note: The first collection of stories about the Baal Shem Tov, compiled by followers after his death; the founding legend of Hasidism.
description: The Baal Shem Tov wrote no books. Shivhei ha-Besht, printed in Hebrew in 1814 and soon in Yiddish, collects some 250 stories about him gathered by Dov Ber of Linits, the son-in-law of the Baal Shem Tov's scribe, and edited by the printer Israel Jaffe. It tells of his hidden years, his revelation as a holy man, his miracles, healings and ascents of the soul, and his encounters with disciples, opponents and ordinary people. Historians use it with care, as legend mingles with memory, but recent research has shown that many figures in it are historical. It is a foundational work of Hasidic storytelling, which became a central genre of Hasidic culture and was later retold by Martin Buber and others.

title: Sermons on Several Occasions
creator: john-wesley
note: Wesley's published sermons, which became the doctrinal standard of Methodism.
description: Wesley issued his sermons in volumes from 1746 onward, writing in plain style 'for plain people'. They include 'Salvation by Faith', preached at Oxford in 1738, 'The Scripture Way of Salvation', 'Christian Perfection', 'The Witness of the Spirit', 'Catholic Spirit' on tolerance between Christians, and 'The Use of Money', with its advice to gain all you can, save all you can and give all you can. The first collections, together with his Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament, became the official doctrinal standards of Methodist preachers and are still referred to by Methodist churches.

title: Journal of John Wesley
creator: john-wesley
note: Wesley's published journal of over fifty years of travel and preaching, including the Aldersgate experience of 1738.
description: Wesley kept a private diary and from 1740 published extracts as his Journal in twenty-one instalments. It records his voyage to Georgia and encounters with the Moravians, his experience at Aldersgate Street on 24 May 1738, when he felt his heart 'strangely warmed', and decades of field preaching across Britain and Ireland, with accounts of mobs, conversions, illnesses and the conditions of the poor. It also reveals his wide reading and interests in medicine and electricity. It is a major source for the history of the revival and of 18th-century social life.

title: Hark! The Herald Angels Sing
creator: charles-wesley
location: First published in Hymns and Sacred Poems, London
note: Charles Wesley's Christmas hymn, adapted by George Whitefield and set to music from Mendelssohn, one of the most popular carols in English.
description: Charles Wesley's original hymn, published in 1739, began 'Hark how all the welkin rings'. George Whitefield altered the first lines in 1753 to the familiar version, and further changes followed. The hymn expresses the theology of the incarnation in compact verse, with lines on Christ 'veiled in flesh' and 'born that man no more may die'. In 1855 the English musician William H. Cummings adapted a melody from a cantata by Felix Mendelssohn to fit it, creating the tune now sung throughout the English-speaking world.

title: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists
creator: charles-wesley
note: The definitive Methodist hymnal, edited by John Wesley and containing mostly Charles's hymns, described as 'a little body of experimental and practical divinity'.
description: In 1780 John Wesley gathered 525 hymns, the great majority by Charles, into a collection organised not by the church year but by the stages of Christian experience: exhortation to sinners, the pleasantness of religion, repentance, seeking for redemption, believers rejoicing, fighting, praying, watching, suffering and seeking full redemption. His preface called it 'a little body of experimental and practical divinity'. It includes hymns such as 'O for a thousand tongues to sing' and 'And can it be'. The collection shaped Methodist worship and theology, and through it the Wesleys' hymns entered the hymnals of many denominations.

title: Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God
creator: jonathan-edwards
location: Preached at Enfield, Connecticut; printed in Boston, 1741
note: Edwards's most famous sermon, preached during the Great Awakening, picturing sinners suspended over the pit of hell by God's mercy alone.
description: Edwards preached this sermon on 8 July 1741 at Enfield, Connecticut, during the Great Awakening. Taking a verse from Deuteronomy, 'their foot shall slide in due time', he argues that only God's mercy keeps unconverted sinners from falling into hell at any moment, using the image of a spider held over a fire. A witness recorded that cries and groans interrupted the preaching. The sermon is often taken as typical of Puritan fire-and-brimstone preaching, though historians note that it was unusual among Edwards's sermons, many of which dwell on the beauty and love of God. It is one of the most anthologised texts of American literature.
image_file: Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God by Jonathan Edwards 1741.jpg
image_caption: Title page of the 1741 Boston printing

title: A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections
creator: jonathan-edwards
note: Edwards's analysis of how to distinguish true from false religious experience, written after the Great Awakening.
description: Faced with both enthusiasm and scepticism after the revivals, Edwards asked what signs show that religious feelings come from God. He argues that true religion consists largely in 'holy affections', yet that intense emotion, bodily effects or fluent religious talk prove nothing either way. He then sets out twelve signs of genuine grace, culminating in a life of Christian practice. Combining Calvinist theology with Lockean psychology, the Religious Affections is a classic of the psychology of religion and influenced later evangelical thinking about conversion, as well as William James.
image_caption: Title page of A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections

title: Jerusalem, or on Religious Power and Judaism
creator: moses-mendelssohn
note: Mendelssohn's argument for freedom of conscience and the separation of religious and state power, with a portrait of Judaism as revealed law.
description: In the first part of Jerusalem, Mendelssohn argues that neither state nor church may coerce belief; the state may compel actions, but religion concerns convictions, so religious bodies should have no power of excommunication or punishment. In the second part, responding to the charge that Judaism itself was a coercive religion, he presents it as a revealed legislation, a law of actions given to Israel, whose eternal truths about God and morality are accessible to all people by reason. He urges Jews to keep the law while taking part in civil society, and calls on states to grant them civil equality. Kant praised the book. It became a founding text of modern Jewish thought and of liberal arguments for religious toleration.
image_caption: Title page of Jerusalem, 1783

title: The Biur (German Torah translation and commentary)
creator: moses-mendelssohn
note: Mendelssohn's German translation of the Torah in Hebrew letters, with a Hebrew commentary by him and his collaborators.
description: Mendelssohn translated the Five Books of Moses into elegant High German, printing it in Hebrew characters so that Jews who read only Hebrew script could learn standard German through a familiar text. The accompanying Hebrew commentary, the Biur ('explanation'), written with collaborators such as Solomon Dubno and Naphtali Herz Wessely, explained the plain meaning using traditional commentaries and grammar. Some rabbis opposed it as an incitement to secular learning, while others approved it. It helped many central European Jews move into German culture and was a landmark of the Haskalah.

title: On Religion: Speeches to its Cultured Despisers
creator: schleiermacher
note: Schleiermacher's Romantic defence of religion as a 'sense and taste for the infinite', addressed to sceptical intellectuals.
description: Written while Schleiermacher was a hospital chaplain in Berlin among the early Romantics, the five speeches address educated people who had rejected religion as superstition or as mere morality. He argues that religion is neither knowledge nor action, but intuition and feeling of the universe, a sense of the infinite in the finite. True religion is found in many forms and in living communities rather than in dogmas or institutions, and Christianity is a supreme but not exclusive expression of it. Revised in later editions, the Speeches marked a new beginning for Protestant theology, shifting attention to religious experience, and influenced the study of religion as a distinct human phenomenon.
image_file: Cover of 1799 edition of Über die Religion.jpg
image_caption: Title page of the first edition of Über die Religion, 1799

title: The Christian Faith (Der christliche Glaube)
creator: schleiermacher
note: Schleiermacher's dogmatics, grounding Christian doctrine in the feeling of absolute dependence and the consciousness of redemption in Christ.
description: In The Christian Faith Schleiermacher defines religion, or piety, as the 'feeling of absolute dependence', consciousness of being in relation with God, and Christianity as the form of piety in which everything is related to the redemption accomplished by Jesus of Nazareth. Doctrines are treated as descriptions of Christian religious self-consciousness, and some traditional teachings, such as the Trinity, which he placed in a conclusion, are reinterpreted. Its method made it the founding work of liberal Protestant theology, and it was the main target of Karl Barth's critique a century later.

title: Fear and Trembling
creator: kierkegaard
location: Published under the pseudonym Johannes de Silentio, Copenhagen
note: A meditation on Abraham's willingness to sacrifice Isaac, asking whether faith can require a 'teleological suspension of the ethical'.
description: Kierkegaard's pseudonymous author, Johannes de Silentio, retells the story of the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22) in several versions and confesses that he cannot understand Abraham. He argues that if Abraham is the father of faith, faith cannot be the same as ethics, the universal duty that would forbid killing one's son; it must involve a 'teleological suspension of the ethical' and an absolute relation of the individual to God, held 'by virtue of the absurd'. He contrasts the 'knight of faith', who gives up everything and receives it back, with the 'knight of infinite resignation'. The book reflects Kierkegaard's own broken engagement and his polemic against Hegelian philosophy and comfortable Christianity, and is a key text for existentialism and for debates in Jewish and Christian thought on the Akedah.
image_caption: Title page of Frygt og Bæven, 1843

title: The Sickness unto Death
creator: kierkegaard
location: Published under the pseudonym Anti-Climacus, Copenhagen
note: Kierkegaard's analysis of despair as the sickness of the self that fails to rest in God.
description: Published under the pseudonym Anti-Climacus, whom Kierkegaard described as a Christian of an extraordinarily high degree, The Sickness unto Death takes its title from Jesus's words about Lazarus. It defines the self as a relation that relates itself to itself and is grounded in the power that established it, and analyses the forms of despair: not being conscious of having a self, not willing to be oneself, and willing defiantly to be oneself. Despair before God is sin, and its opposite is faith. The work's psychological depth influenced Heidegger, Sartre and theologians such as Tillich and Barth.
image_caption: Title page of Sygdommen til Døden, 1849

title: Apologia Pro Vita Sua
creator: newman
note: Newman's account of the history of his religious opinions and his journey from Anglicanism to Roman Catholicism.
description: In January 1864 the novelist Charles Kingsley wrote that truth for its own sake had never been a virtue of the Roman clergy, citing Newman. Newman responded first with an exchange of letters and then, in seven weekly pamphlets written at great speed, with a history of his religious opinions: his evangelical conversion as a boy, his Oxford years, the Oxford Movement and the Tracts for the Times, his growing doubts about the Anglican claim, and his reception into the Catholic Church in 1845. The candour and beauty of the book won wide admiration in Victorian England and restored his reputation. It is a classic of English autobiography and of religious literature.
image_file: Title page of the first edition of Apologia Pro Vita Sua.jpg
image_caption: Title page of the first edition, 1864

title: An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine
creator: newman
note: Newman's argument that Christian doctrine develops organically over time, written on the eve of his conversion to Catholicism.
description: Newman wrote the Essay while trying to decide whether the Roman Catholic Church was the true heir of the early church, despite doctrines not explicitly found in scripture or the early Fathers. He argued that living ideas unfold over time, as an acorn becomes an oak, and proposed seven 'notes' for distinguishing true developments from corruptions, such as preservation of type, continuity of principles and chronic vigour. He finished it before his reception into the Catholic Church in October 1845. Controversial at first among both Protestants and Catholics, the idea of doctrinal development became widely influential, and is reflected in the Second Vatican Council.

title: Nineteen Letters on Judaism
creator: samson-raphael-hirsch
note: Hirsch's letters from a young rabbi to a doubting friend, setting out a modern defence of traditional Judaism.
description: Published under the pseudonym Ben Uziel, the Nineteen Letters respond to Benjamin, a young Jew drawn to European culture who doubts the value of the commandments. Hirsch's rabbi, Naphtali, explains Judaism as a divinely given way of life whose laws educate humanity toward justice and service of God, argues that the Jewish mission in exile is to witness to God among the nations, and calls for a renewal of Jewish education rooted in the Torah but open to general culture. Appearing as Reform Judaism was gaining ground in Germany, it became a manifesto of Neo-Orthodoxy.

title: The Varieties of Religious Experience
creator: william-james
location: Gifford Lectures, University of Edinburgh, 1901–02; published New York and London
note: James's study of conversion, saintliness and mysticism through personal testimony, a founding classic of the study of religion.
description: Delivered as Gifford Lectures in Edinburgh, the Varieties defines religion, for his purposes, as the feelings, acts and experiences of individuals in relation to whatever they consider the divine. Drawing on autobiographies of saints, mystics, converts and ordinary people, James contrasts the 'healthy-minded' with the 'sick soul' and the 'twice-born', and analyses conversion, saintliness and mysticism, proposing four marks of mystical experience: ineffability, a noetic quality, transiency and passivity. Judging religion pragmatically by its fruits, he concludes that it is open to the reality of a 'more' beyond conscious life. The book has remained continuously in print.

title: The Quest of the Historical Jesus
creator: schweitzer
location: Published as Von Reimarus zu Wrede, Tübingen
note: Schweitzer's survey of a century of lives of Jesus, arguing that Jesus was an apocalyptic prophet expecting the end of the world.
description: Originally titled From Reimarus to Wrede, the book reviews German and other scholarship from H. S. Reimarus in the 18th century to William Wrede in 1901, showing how each liberal 'life of Jesus' had made him in the image of its author's ideals. Schweitzer argued that the historical Jesus was dominated by the expectation of the imminent kingdom of God and, when it did not come, went to his death to bring it about, a figure strange to modern people. The book effectively ended the 19th-century quest and set the agenda for later debates on eschatology, and the 'new quest' and 'third quest' of the historical Jesus took up its questions.

title: I and Thou (Ich und Du)
creator: buber
note: Buber's poetic treatise on the two basic attitudes, I–It and I–Thou, and on God as the eternal Thou.
description: In three parts written in aphoristic prose, Buber argues that human existence is lived in two primary relations. In I–It, we experience and use things and people as objects; in I–Thou, we meet the other in the fullness of presence, in mutuality and without purpose. Such encounters with nature, with other people and with spiritual forms are fleeting, and every Thou becomes an It again, but in each we glimpse the eternal Thou, God, who can only be addressed, not expressed. The book influenced Jewish and Christian theologians, existentialist philosophers, educators and psychotherapists. It remains under copyright and is available in English translations by Ronald Gregor Smith (1937) and Walter Kaufmann (1970).

title: Tales of the Hasidim
creator: buber
note: Buber's retellings of stories of the Hasidic masters, which introduced Hasidism to a wide modern readership.
description: From his first books in 1906 onward, Buber retold the stories of the Hasidic rabbis, from the Baal Shem Tov to the masters of the 19th century, in polished German prose. The two-volume Tales of the Hasidim (The Early Masters and The Later Masters) brings together his mature collection, with introductions explaining the movement's spirit. Buber presented Hasidism as a joyful hallowing of everyday life. Scholars such as Gershom Scholem argued that he neglected its theological and legal teachings, but the books shaped the image of Hasidism for generations of readers.

title: The Epistle to the Romans (Der Römerbrief)
creator: barth
note: Barth's explosive commentary on Romans, which broke with liberal theology and launched dialectical theology.
description: Written while Barth was a village pastor in Safenwil, the commentary rejected the historical-critical approach and liberal theology of his teachers, reading Paul as speaking directly to the present about the 'infinite qualitative distinction' between God and humanity, a phrase borrowed from Kierkegaard. The completely rewritten second edition of 1922 was even more radical, describing God's revelation as a crisis that judges all human religion, culture and morality. The Catholic theologian Karl Adam said it fell 'like a bomb on the playground of the theologians'. It launched the movement known as dialectical theology or neo-orthodoxy.

title: Church Dogmatics (Die kirchliche Dogmatik)
creator: barth
note: Barth's monumental, unfinished theology in thirteen part-volumes, the most extensive Protestant dogmatics of the 20th century.
description: Barth began the Church Dogmatics in Bonn in 1932 and continued it in Basel until 1967, producing over 9,000 pages in four volumes divided into thirteen part-volumes: the Word of God, the doctrine of God, creation and reconciliation; a planned fifth volume on redemption was never written. Everything is centred on God's self-revelation in Jesus Christ. Among its most influential parts are its reconstruction of the doctrine of election, in which Christ is both the electing God and the elected human being, and its extensive small-print discussions of the Bible and the history of theology. It is widely studied by Protestant and Catholic theologians.

title: Barmen Theological Declaration
creator: barth
note: The declaration of the Confessing Church rejecting Nazi control of the German Protestant churches, largely drafted by Barth.
description: In May 1934 representatives of Lutheran, Reformed and United churches met at Barmen in Wuppertal to oppose the 'German Christians', who supported Nazi ideology and sought to bring the church under the Reich. Its six theses, largely drafted by Barth, declare that Jesus Christ is the one Word of God that the church must obey, rejecting other sources of revelation and the claim of the state to be the church's master. It does not explicitly mention the persecution of the Jews, an omission later criticised by many, including Barth himself. The Declaration became the founding document of the Confessing Church and has been adopted as a confessional standard by several churches.
image_caption: West German postage stamp marking the 50th anniversary of the Barmen Declaration, 1984

title: Systematic Theology
creator: tillich
note: Tillich's three-volume theology correlating existential questions with Christian symbols, God as 'being itself'.
description: In three volumes, Tillich uses a 'method of correlation' in which philosophy formulates the questions arising from human existence, such as finitude, estrangement and ambiguity, and theology answers with the symbols of Christian revelation. Its five parts treat reason and revelation, being and God, existence and the Christ, life and the Spirit, and history and the kingdom of God. Tillich describes God not as a being among others but as 'being itself' or the 'ground of being', and Christ as the 'New Being'. The work was influential in mid-century American theology and in dialogue with psychology and the arts.

title: Discipleship (The Cost of Discipleship)
creator: bonhoeffer
note: Bonhoeffer's exposition of the Sermon on the Mount, contrasting 'cheap grace' with the costly grace of following Christ.
description: Written from his teaching at the illegal Confessing Church seminary at Finkenwalde, Nachfolge ('Discipleship') opens with the famous distinction between cheap grace, 'grace without discipleship', which the church sells cheaply as an assurance without demands, and costly grace, which calls a person to follow Jesus at the cost of one's life. Much of the book expounds the Sermon on the Mount. Published in 1937, the year the Gestapo closed the seminary, it was translated into English in 1948 as The Cost of Discipleship, and Bonhoeffer's execution gave its words exceptional authority.

title: Letters and Papers from Prison
creator: bonhoeffer
location: Written in Tegel prison, Berlin; edited by Eberhard Bethge, Munich
note: Bonhoeffer's prison letters and notes, with his searching questions about 'religionless Christianity' in a world come of age.
description: After his arrest in April 1943, Bonhoeffer wrote letters to his family and above all to his friend Eberhard Bethge, smuggled out by sympathetic guards, as well as poems such as 'Who am I?' and 'By gracious powers'. From April 1944 the letters explore new theological ideas: that the world has 'come of age' and no longer needs God as a stopgap, that Christianity must be 'religionless', and that the church must exist for others. Bethge published them in 1951 as Widerstand und Ergebung ('Resistance and Submission'). Their fragmentary, provocative thoughts stimulated the 'secular theology' of the 1960s and continue to be debated.

title: Letter from Birmingham Jail
creator: martin-luther-king
location: Written in Birmingham City Jail, Alabama
note: King's reply to white clergymen who called the civil rights protests 'unwise and untimely', a classic defence of nonviolent direct action.
description: Arrested on 12 April 1963 during the Birmingham campaign against segregation, King read a statement by eight white Alabama clergymen urging Black citizens to stop demonstrating and wait for the courts. Writing at first in the margins of a newspaper, he answered that injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere, that nonviolent direct action aims to create tension that forces negotiation, and that one has a moral duty to disobey unjust laws, citing Augustine and Aquinas. He expressed disappointment with the 'white moderate' and with churches that stayed silent. The letter, widely published that summer, became one of the most important documents of the civil rights movement and of Christian social ethics. It remains under copyright and is reproduced by The King Center and the Martin Luther King Jr. Research and Education Institute at Stanford.
image_file: Recreation of Martin Luther King's Cell in Birmingham Jail - National Civil Rights Museum - Downtown Memphis - Tennessee - USA.jpg
image_caption: Recreation of King's cell in the Birmingham jail, National Civil Rights Museum, Memphis

title: Strength to Love
creator: martin-luther-king
note: A collection of King's sermons on love, justice, fear and faith, including 'Loving Your Enemies'.
description: Strength to Love gathers sixteen sermons, many preached at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery and Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta, and revised partly while King was in jail. They include 'A Tough Mind and a Tender Heart', 'Loving Your Enemies', 'Antidotes for Fear' and 'Pilgrimage to Nonviolence', in which he describes his intellectual journey through the social gospel, Niebuhr and Gandhi. The book shows the theological foundations of King's activism in the Black church preaching tradition. It remains under copyright.

title: Pacem in terris
creator: john-xxiii
note: John XXIII's encyclical on peace and human rights, addressed for the first time to 'all men of good will'.
description: Issued in April 1963, two months before his death and months after the Cuban missile crisis, Pacem in terris sets out a vision of peace founded on truth, justice, charity and freedom. It lists universal human rights, including freedom of religion and conscience, and corresponding duties, discusses relations between individuals and states and among nations, calls for disarmament and the banning of nuclear weapons, and supports the United Nations. It was the first encyclical addressed not only to Catholics but to all people of good will, and it was widely welcomed, influencing the Second Vatican Council and later Catholic social teaching.

title: Documents of the Second Vatican Council
creator: church-councils
note: Sixteen documents that reshaped Catholic worship, its understanding of the church and its relations with other Christians, other religions and the modern world.
description: Convened by John XXIII and continued under Paul VI, the Second Vatican Council brought some 2,500 bishops to Rome in four sessions from 1962 to 1965, with Protestant and Orthodox observers present. Its sixteen documents include four constitutions: on the liturgy (Sacrosanctum concilium), which permitted the use of vernacular languages in the Mass; on the church (Lumen gentium), emphasising the church as the people of God and the collegiality of bishops; on revelation (Dei verbum); and on the church in the modern world (Gaudium et spes). The declaration Nostra aetate (1965) repudiated the charge that the Jews as a people were collectively guilty for Christ's death and spoke respectfully of Islam and other religions, and Dignitatis humanae affirmed religious freedom. How to interpret the council's reforms, as continuity or rupture, remains debated within Catholicism.

title: Sarajevo Haggadah
creator: jewish-illuminators
location: National Museum of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sarajevo
note: A richly illuminated Passover Haggadah from Catalonia that survived the expulsion from Spain and the wars of the 20th century.
description: The Sarajevo Haggadah was made in Catalonia, probably Barcelona, around 1350. Besides the text of the Passover service, it contains thirty-four full-page miniatures in gold and colour, from the creation of the world to the death of Moses, together with a picture of a Spanish synagogue. It probably left Spain with refugees after the expulsion of 1492, and notes in it show that it was in Italy in 1609, when a Catholic censor approved it. It was sold to the National Museum in Sarajevo in 1894. During the Second World War it was hidden from the Nazis, according to the best-known account, by the museum's Muslim librarian Derviš Korkut; it survived again during the siege of Sarajevo in the 1990s. Its story inspired Geraldine Brooks's novel People of the Book.
image_caption: The Sarajevo Haggadah

title: Golden Haggadah
creator: jewish-illuminators
note: A sumptuous Passover Haggadah from Catalonia, its biblical scenes painted against gold-leaf backgrounds.
description: The Golden Haggadah was made in or near Barcelona in the early 14th century. Its fourteen pages of miniatures, with scenes from Genesis and Exodus arranged in four panels per page against tooled gold backgrounds, are in the Gothic style of the time and show the involvement of at least two artists, perhaps working in a Christian workshop. Further images show Passover preparations, such as cleaning the house of leaven and distributing matzah. An inscription records that it was given as a wedding gift in Italy in 1602. It entered the British Museum in 1865 and is now in the British Library.
image_caption: A page of the Golden Haggadah (British Library)

title: Aleppo Codex
creator: masoretes
location: Israel Museum (Shrine of the Book), Jerusalem
note: The most authoritative manuscript of the Masoretic Hebrew Bible, vocalised in Tiberias; about a third was lost in 1947.
description: The Aleppo Codex is a parchment codex of the whole Hebrew Bible written around 930 in Tiberias. Its consonantal text was copied by the scribe Shlomo ben Buya'a, and the vowel points, accents and Masoretic notes were added, according to its colophon, by Aaron ben Asher, the leading Masorete of his day. Maimonides is believed to have used it when he set out rules for writing Torah scrolls, which gave it unique prestige. After passing through Jerusalem and Cairo it was kept for some five centuries by the Jewish community of Aleppo in Syria. During riots in December 1947 the synagogue was burned and large parts of the codex, including most of the Torah, went missing; the surviving leaves were smuggled to Israel in 1957–58. It is the basis of the Hebrew University Bible Project edition, and the fate of the missing pages remains the subject of investigation.
image_caption: Aleppo Codex, the opening of the Book of Joshua

title: Leningrad Codex
creator: masoretes
location: National Library of Russia, St Petersburg
note: The oldest complete manuscript of the Hebrew Bible in the Masoretic tradition, basis of the standard scholarly editions.
description: Copied in Cairo around 1008–1010 by the scribe Samuel ben Jacob, who states that he corrected it according to manuscripts of the Ben Asher school, the Leningrad Codex contains the entire Hebrew Bible with vowels, accents and Masoretic notes. It also includes 'carpet pages' of geometric decoration, with micrographic Masoretic notes written in tiny letters forming patterns. The manuscript was acquired by the Karaite collector Abraham Firkovich and came to the Imperial Public Library in St Petersburg in the 19th century. Because the Aleppo Codex is incomplete, the Leningrad Codex is the basis of the scholarly editions Biblia Hebraica (from its third edition, 1937), Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia and Biblia Hebraica Quinta, and so of most modern translations of the Old Testament.
image_caption: Leningrad Codex, folio 474a, a decorated 'carpet page'

title: Septuagint
creator: septuagint-translators
location: Alexandria; preserved in codices such as Sinaiticus and Vaticanus
note: The Greek translation of the Jewish scriptures, the Bible of Hellenistic Jews and the Old Testament of the early church.
description: The Septuagint, often abbreviated LXX, is the collection of Greek translations of the Hebrew scriptures made by Jewish translators from the 3rd century BC, beginning with the Torah in Alexandria. The translation varies from very literal to quite free, and in some books, such as Jeremiah, it reflects a Hebrew text different from the later Masoretic one, as Dead Sea Scrolls fragments have confirmed. It also includes works composed in Greek or surviving only in Greek, such as the Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach in translation, Judith, Tobit and the books of Maccabees. The New Testament writers usually quote scripture from it, and it remained the Old Testament of the Greek-speaking church, used today by the Orthodox. Its additional books were kept by Catholics and Orthodox but placed in an Apocrypha or removed by Protestants. The oldest complete copies are in the great 4th- and 5th-century Christian codices.
image_file: Codex Vaticanus (1 Esdras 1-55 to 2-5) (The S.S. Teacher's Edition-The Holy Bible).jpg
image_caption: A page of the Septuagint in Codex Vaticanus (1 Esdras), from a 19th-century reproduction

title: Dead Sea Scrolls
creator: qumran-community
location: Israel Museum (Shrine of the Book), Jerusalem; Jordan Museum, Amman; and other collections
note: Some 900 manuscripts, biblical and sectarian, found in caves near Qumran from 1947, the oldest surviving copies of the Hebrew Bible.
description: The first scrolls were found in 1946–47 by Bedouin shepherds in a cave near Khirbet Qumran; by 1956 eleven caves had yielded tens of thousands of fragments from roughly 900 manuscripts, mostly on parchment, in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek. They date from about the 3rd century BC to the 1st century AD. Around a quarter are copies of biblical books, every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther being represented, about a thousand years older than the previously known medieval manuscripts. Others are previously unknown texts: rules for a community, hymns, calendars, commentaries on prophets and apocalyptic works such as the War Scroll. The identity of the people who collected them, most often identified with the Essenes, is debated, as is the relationship between the scrolls and the nearby settlement. The slow publication of the fragments caused controversy until full access was granted in 1991. The scrolls have reshaped the study of the Hebrew Bible's text and of the Jewish world in which Christianity began.
image_file: Dead Sea Scroll, Pesher Isaiah, from Qumran Cave 4. The Jordan Museum, Amman.jpg
image_caption: Pesher (commentary) on Isaiah from Qumran Cave 4 (The Jordan Museum, Amman)

title: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a)
creator: qumran-community
location: Israel Museum (Shrine of the Book), Jerusalem
note: A complete copy of the Book of Isaiah, the best preserved of the Dead Sea Scrolls and among the oldest biblical manuscripts.
description: Found in Qumran Cave 1 in 1947, the Great Isaiah Scroll consists of seventeen sheets of parchment sewn together into a scroll over seven metres long, containing all sixty-six chapters of Isaiah in fifty-four columns. Palaeography and radiocarbon dating place it in the 2nd century BC. Its text agrees substantially with the medieval Masoretic Text, though it has thousands of minor variants in spelling and some significant differences in wording, illuminating how carefully, and with how much variation, scripture was copied. It was one of the first scrolls sold, through a dealer in Bethlehem, to the Syrian Orthodox metropolitan of Jerusalem, who later sold it to Israel in 1954. A facsimile is displayed in the Shrine of the Book, and the scroll can be viewed online in high resolution.
image_file: The Great Isaiah Scroll MS A (1QIsa) - Google Art Project.jpg
image_caption: The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a), Israel Museum, Jerusalem

title: Community Rule (Serekh ha-Yahad)
creator: qumran-community
location: Israel Museum (Shrine of the Book), Jerusalem
note: The rulebook of a Jewish community that called itself the Yahad, describing admission, discipline and the struggle of light and darkness.
description: The best-preserved copy of the Community Rule, from Qumran Cave 1, was among the first scrolls discovered; further copies from Cave 4 show that the text developed over time. It describes how members entered a covenant, surrendered property to the community, passed through stages of probation, shared meals and study, and were punished for offences such as speaking against fellow members. A famous section, the Treatise on the Two Spirits, teaches that humanity is divided between a spirit of truth and a spirit of falsehood until God's final visitation. The text's parallels with ancient descriptions of the Essenes underlie the common identification of the Qumran group with them. Scholars have also compared its practices with those of the early Christian community in Acts, though direct links are not established.

title: On the Creation of the World (De opificio mundi)
creator: philo
location: Alexandria; preserved in Byzantine Greek manuscripts
note: Philo's reading of the creation account in Genesis through Platonic philosophy, the first sustained philosophical commentary on scripture.
description: In this treatise Philo interprets the first chapters of Genesis as a philosophical account of the cosmos. He argues that the six days are not a time sequence but an expression of order, that God first conceived an intelligible world of ideas, located in the divine Logos, and then made the visible world in its image, much as an architect plans a city before building it. The work, which draws on Plato's Timaeus and on Stoic and Pythagorean ideas, including number symbolism, opens Philo's series on the laws of Moses, presenting Moses as the supreme philosopher. Its approach of reading scripture alongside Greek philosophy was taken up by Christian writers such as Clement, Origen and Ambrose, and helped shape centuries of Christian commentary on creation.

title: On the Contemplative Life
creator: philo
note: Philo's description of the Therapeutae, a community of Jewish men and women devoted to prayer and study near Lake Mareotis in Egypt.
description: Philo describes a group he calls the Therapeutae ('healers' or 'worshippers'), who had left property and family to live in simple dwellings outside Alexandria, studying scripture allegorically during the week and gathering on the seventh day, men and women separately, with a great festival every fiftieth day including a night of choral singing. It is the only ancient description of this group. Eusebius in the 4th century believed they were early Christian monks, an identification no longer accepted; some modern scholars have even questioned whether Philo idealised them. The treatise is an important witness to Jewish ascetic piety in the Second Temple period and to the role of women in it, and it later fed Christian ideals of monastic life.

title: The Jewish War
creator: josephus
location: Rome; preserved in Greek manuscripts and an early Latin translation
note: A first-hand history of the Jewish revolt against Rome and the destruction of Jerusalem and its Temple in AD 70.
description: Josephus wrote the Jewish War in Rome in the 70s AD, first, he says, in Aramaic for Jews of the east and then in Greek. After surveying Jewish history from the Maccabees through Herod the Great, it narrates the revolt from its outbreak in 66, Josephus's own command in Galilee, the factional strife in Jerusalem, the siege and burning of the Temple by Titus in 70, and the fall of Masada, where he reports the defenders' mass suicide. Its description of the Temple, the Jewish sects and the Roman army are invaluable. Josephus writes as a client of the Flavian emperors, blaming the disaster on rebel fanatics rather than on the Jewish people or on Rome, and historians weigh his account with that in mind. Christians read the fall of Jerusalem as fulfilling the prophecies of Jesus, and the book was widely copied and translated in the Middle Ages.
image_caption: An edition of the Jewish War printed in 1559

title: Jewish Antiquities
creator: josephus
note: A history of the Jewish people from creation to the eve of the revolt, written for Greek and Roman readers, with famous references to John the Baptist, James and Jesus.
description: In twenty books, the Antiquities retells the biblical story, adding traditions found elsewhere in Jewish sources, and continues the history through the Persian, Hellenistic and Roman periods, with extensive detail on the Hasmoneans, Herod and the Roman governors of Judea. Josephus's aim was to present Judaism as an ancient and honourable nation to a gentile audience. Book 18 contains a brief account of Jesus, the Testimonium Flavianum; in its transmitted form it calls Jesus the Messiah, which most scholars consider a Christian interpolation, though many think Josephus wrote a shorter, neutral notice. A passage on the death of 'James, the brother of Jesus who was called Christ' in Book 20 is generally accepted as authentic. The work is a major source for the historical context of the New Testament.
image_file: Flavius Josephus, Antiquitates Iudaicae, Florence, Plut. 66.5.jpg
image_caption: A manuscript of the Jewish Antiquities, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Florence (Plut. 66.5)

title: Gospel of Mark
creator: gospel-writers
note: The shortest and, most scholars think, earliest Gospel: a fast-paced account of Jesus's ministry, death and empty tomb.
description: Mark begins abruptly with John the Baptist and Jesus's baptism, and moves rapidly, often linking scenes with 'immediately', through Jesus's healings, exorcisms, parables and conflicts in Galilee to his journey to Jerusalem, his passion and his death on the cross. Throughout, Jesus tells those who recognise him to keep silent, a theme scholars call the 'messianic secret'. The earliest manuscripts end at 16:8, with women fleeing the empty tomb in fear; the longer endings found in later manuscripts are generally regarded as additions. Early tradition, reported by Papias in the 2nd century, held that Mark was Peter's interpreter in Rome; modern scholars date it around the Jewish war of 66–73, and debate whether it was written in Rome, Syria or Galilee. Most accept 'Markan priority', the view that Matthew and Luke used Mark as a source, which made this neglected Gospel central to modern study of the historical Jesus.
image_caption: Mark 16 in Codex Sinaiticus, 4th century

title: Gospel of Matthew
creator: gospel-writers
note: The Gospel that presents Jesus as the fulfilment of Jewish scripture and contains the Sermon on the Mount and the Lord's Prayer.
description: Matthew opens with a genealogy tracing Jesus to Abraham and David and with the stories of the Magi and the flight into Egypt. It arranges Jesus's teaching into five great discourses, beginning with the Sermon on the Mount, which contains the Beatitudes and the Lord's Prayer, and repeatedly notes how events fulfil the prophets. It ends with the risen Jesus commissioning his disciples to make disciples of all nations. Placed first in the New Testament, it was the most quoted Gospel in the early church. Tradition attributed it to the apostle Matthew, the tax collector; most scholars think its author was an anonymous Jewish-Christian writer around 80–90 who used Mark and the sayings source Q. Its sharp polemic against the Pharisees reflects tensions between the early church and the synagogue, and some of its verses were later used to justify Christian hostility toward Jews, a history that modern churches have confronted.
image_file: Oxford, Sackler Library Ms LXIV 4404 (Papyrus 104) recto Matt 21, 34-37.jpg
image_caption: Papyrus 104, an early fragment of Matthew 21 (Sackler Library, Oxford)

title: Gospel of Luke and Acts of the Apostles
creator: gospel-writers
note: A two-volume narrative from the birth of Jesus to Paul's arrival in Rome, with the parables of the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son.
description: Luke and Acts, addressed to a certain Theophilus, were written as a single work by the same author. The Gospel gives the fullest account of Jesus's birth, with the annunciation, the shepherds and the canticles of Mary and Zechariah, and includes parables found only in Luke, such as the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son, with a marked concern for the poor, women and outsiders. Acts continues with the ascension, the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost, the growth of the Jerusalem church, and the missions of Peter and above all Paul, ending with Paul preaching under house arrest in Rome. Tradition identified the author as Luke, the physician and companion of Paul; the 'we' passages in Acts have been read as eyewitness memory or as a literary device. Most scholars date the work to around 80–95. Acts is the main source, though one whose historical reliability is debated, for the first decades of the church.
image_caption: Luke 13–14 in a 3rd-century papyrus codex (Chester Beatty Library, Dublin)

title: Gospel of John
creator: gospel-writers
note: The most theological Gospel, opening 'In the beginning was the Word' and presenting Jesus as the incarnate Son revealing the Father.
description: John differs markedly from the other three, 'synoptic', Gospels. It begins with a hymn to the Logos, the Word who was with God and became flesh, and arranges Jesus's ministry around seven 'signs', such as turning water into wine at Cana and raising Lazarus, and long discourses with 'I am' sayings: the bread of life, the light of the world, the good shepherd. Its chronology, with several visits to Jerusalem, also differs. The Gospel refers to an anonymous 'disciple whom Jesus loved' as its witness; tradition identified him with the apostle John, writing at Ephesus in old age. Many scholars instead think of a 'Johannine community' whose traditions were edited in stages and completed around 90–110. Its high Christology was decisive for later doctrine of the Trinity, and its depiction of 'the Jews' as opponents is much discussed in modern Jewish-Christian dialogue.
image_caption: Rylands Papyrus P52, a small early fragment of John 18 (John Rylands Library, Manchester)

title: Epistle to the Romans
creator: paul
location: Written in Corinth to the church in Rome
note: Paul's longest and most systematic letter, on sin, grace, justification by faith and the place of Israel, the most influential text of Protestant theology.
description: Paul wrote Romans, probably from Corinth around 57, to a church he had not founded, preparing for a visit on his way to Spain. He argues that all people, Jews and gentiles, have fallen short and are made righteous by God through faith in Christ, not by works of the law; that believers die and rise with Christ in baptism and live by the Spirit; and, in chapters 9–11, that God has not abandoned Israel, which will ultimately be saved. The letter ends with ethical exhortation and greetings to many named individuals, including women such as Phoebe and Junia. Romans was pivotal for Augustine's conversion and for Luther, Calvin and Barth. Since the 1970s the 'New Perspective on Paul' has argued that Paul was addressing the inclusion of gentiles more than individual guilt, a reading that remains debated.
image_caption: Uncial 0220, an early parchment leaf of Romans 4–5

title: First Epistle to the Corinthians
creator: paul
location: Written in Ephesus to the church in Corinth
note: Paul's practical letter to a divided church, including the hymn to love, the earliest account of the Lord's Supper and of the resurrection appearances.
description: Paul wrote this letter from Ephesus to the church he had founded in Corinth, a cosmopolitan Greek port, in response to reports of factions and to questions the Corinthians had sent him. He addresses rivalries among followers of different leaders, sexual morality, marriage and celibacy, eating food offered to idols, the conduct of worship and spiritual gifts such as speaking in tongues. Chapter 11 contains the earliest written account of the words of Jesus at the Last Supper, and chapter 15 lists witnesses of the risen Christ and argues for the bodily resurrection. Chapter 13, 'love is patient, love is kind', is among the best-known passages in the Bible. The letter offers a rare window into the life of an early Christian community. Some passages, notably on women keeping silent in church, are debated, with some scholars considering them later insertions.
image_file: Ann Arbor, University of Michigan P.Mich.inv. 6238 (Papyrus 46) fol. 79v 1 Cor 2, 11–3, 5.jpg
image_caption: 1 Corinthians 2–3 in Papyrus 46, c. 200 (University of Michigan)

title: Epistle to the Galatians
creator: paul
location: Written to churches in Galatia, Asia Minor
note: Paul's fiery defence of his gospel against those who required gentile converts to be circumcised.
description: Galatians was written to churches in central Asia Minor that had been visited by teachers insisting that gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the Jewish law. Paul responds with an autobiographical account of his call and his dealings with the Jerusalem apostles, including a confrontation with Peter at Antioch, and argues that people are justified by faith, as Abraham was, so that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male and female. Its date is debated, some placing it among his earliest letters around 48 and others in the mid-50s. Luther called it his favourite letter, and it was central to Reformation debates about law and gospel.
image_file: Ann Arbor, University of Michigan P.Mich.inv. 6238 (Papyrus 46) fol. 158r Eph 6, 20–Gal 1, 8.jpg
image_caption: The end of Ephesians and opening of Galatians in Papyrus 46, c. 200 (University of Michigan)

title: Book of Revelation
creator: john-of-patmos
location: Written on Patmos to seven churches of Asia Minor
note: The final book of the Christian Bible: visions of heavenly worship, cosmic conflict, the fall of Babylon and a new heaven and new earth.
description: Revelation, or the Apocalypse, opens with letters from the risen Christ to seven churches in western Asia Minor and then unfolds a series of visions: the throne of God surrounded by living creatures, the Lamb opening a scroll with seven seals, trumpets and bowls of judgement, the woman clothed with the sun, the dragon and the beast whose number is 666, the fall of 'Babylon the great', the thousand-year reign of Christ, the last judgement and the descent of the New Jerusalem. Its imagery draws heavily on Ezekiel, Daniel and other prophets. Most scholars read it as addressed to Christians under the pressures of Roman imperial cult around 95, with Babylon standing for Rome. Its place in the canon was disputed for centuries, especially in the East. It has inspired countless interpretations of history and the end times, as well as Dürer's woodcuts, medieval tapestries and the language of Handel's Messiah.
image_file: Dublin, Chester Beatty Ms Chester Beatty III Papyrus 47 fol. 7r Rev 13,16-14.jpg
image_caption: Revelation 13–14 in Papyrus 47, 3rd century (Chester Beatty Library, Dublin)

title: Didache
creator: early-christian-scribes
location: Probably Syria; the only complete text is a manuscript of 1056, Jerusalem
note: 'The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles', the oldest surviving manual of Christian ethics, baptism, prayer and community life.
description: The Didache is a short anonymous Greek text in sixteen chapters. It begins with the 'two ways' of life and death, an ethical teaching with Jewish roots, then gives instructions for baptism, preferably in running water, for fasting on Wednesdays and Fridays, for saying the Lord's Prayer three times a day, and for the eucharist, with prayers of thanksgiving over the cup and bread. It also regulates the treatment of travelling apostles and prophets and ends with warnings about the last days. It was known by name to early writers but lost until Philotheos Bryennios, a Greek Orthodox metropolitan, found it in 1873 in a manuscript in Constantinople, publishing it in 1883. Its date is debated, many scholars placing it around the end of the 1st century, and it is a key witness to Christian practice in the generation after the apostles.
image_caption: A page of the Didache

title: Gospel of Thomas
creator: early-christian-scribes
location: Coptic version in the Nag Hammadi codices, Coptic Museum, Cairo; Greek fragments from Oxyrhynchus
note: A collection of 114 sayings attributed to Jesus, found complete at Nag Hammadi, some paralleling the Gospels and others unknown.
description: The Gospel of Thomas presents itself as the 'secret sayings which the living Jesus spoke and which Didymos Judas Thomas wrote down'. It has no narrative of Jesus's birth, miracles, death or resurrection, only sayings, many introduced simply with 'Jesus said'. About half have parallels in the synoptic Gospels, such as the parable of the sower, while others have a mystical cast, speaking of finding the kingdom within and of knowing oneself. Greek fragments found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt in the 1890s were identified only after the complete Coptic text came to light at Nag Hammadi in 1945. Scholars sharply debate its date and relation to the canonical Gospels: some see it as preserving independent early traditions, others as a 2nd-century work dependent on them. It was not accepted into the New Testament.
