image_caption: The opening of the Gospel of Thomas in Nag Hammadi Codex II

title: Nag Hammadi library
creator: early-christian-scribes
year: 4th century AD (copies of texts from the 2nd–3rd centuries)
note: Thirteen leather-bound Coptic codices discovered in Upper Egypt in 1945, containing Gnostic and other early Christian texts.
description: In December 1945 farmers digging near the town of Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt found a jar containing thirteen papyrus codices bound in leather, with some fifty texts translated into Coptic from Greek. They include the Gospel of Thomas, the Gospel of Philip, the Gospel of Truth, the Apocryphon of John and other works, many associated with the varied movements later grouped as Gnosticism, which taught salvation through secret knowledge and often distinguished the supreme God from a lower creator. The codices were probably copied in the 4th century and may have been buried by monks of a nearby Pachomian monastery, though this is debated. Before the discovery these movements were known mainly through their opponents, such as Irenaeus. The find, published fully in the 1970s, transformed scholarship on the diversity of early Christianity.
image_caption: Nag Hammadi Codex II (Coptic Museum, Cairo)

title: Codex Sinaiticus
creator: early-christian-scribes
location: British Library, London; with leaves in Leipzig, St Catherine's Monastery (Sinai) and St Petersburg
note: A 4th-century handwritten Greek Bible, containing the oldest complete New Testament.
description: Codex Sinaiticus was written on parchment by several scribes in the mid-4th century, perhaps in Caesarea or Egypt, in four columns per page in Greek capitals. It originally contained the whole Septuagint Old Testament, of which about half survives, and the complete New Testament, together with the Epistle of Barnabas and part of the Shepherd of Hermas. It was kept for centuries at St Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai. The German scholar Constantin von Tischendorf took leaves from the monastery in 1844 and the bulk of the codex in 1859, which was then presented to the Russian tsar; the circumstances remain contested by the monastery. In 1933 the Soviet government sold it to the British Museum. It bears thousands of later corrections, a valuable record of how the text was revised. In 2009 the dispersed parts were digitally reunited online, and it is one of the most important witnesses to the text of the Bible.
image_caption: A page of Codex Sinaiticus

title: Codex Vaticanus
creator: early-christian-scribes
note: Probably the oldest nearly complete manuscript of the Greek Bible, held in the Vatican Library since at least the 15th century.
description: Codex Vaticanus (Vat. gr. 1209) is a parchment codex written in three columns per page by two or three scribes, dated by palaeographers to the first half of the 4th century. It contains most of the Septuagint and the New Testament up to Hebrews 9:14; the end of the New Testament, including the pastoral letters and Revelation, is lost, and later hands supplied some missing parts. It is recorded in the Vatican Library's first catalogue of 1475. Scholars restricted from studying it for centuries came to recognise its exceptional textual quality. The New Testament text of Westcott and Hort (1881), and through it most modern critical editions and translations, relies heavily on Vaticanus together with Sinaiticus.
image_caption: Codex Vaticanus, the end of 2 Thessalonians and the beginning of Hebrews

title: Rossano Gospels
creator: early-christian-scribes
note: One of the oldest surviving illustrated Gospel books, written in silver on purple parchment with vivid scenes of Christ's life.
description: The Codex Purpureus Rossanensis contains the Gospels of Matthew and most of Mark in Greek, written in silver and gold ink on parchment dyed purple, a colour associated with imperial luxury. It was probably made in the eastern Mediterranean, perhaps Syria or Constantinople, in the 6th century. Its fourteen surviving full-page miniatures show scenes such as the raising of Lazarus, the entry into Jerusalem, the Last Supper, Christ before Pilate and the parable of the wise and foolish virgins, often accompanied by Old Testament prophets pointing to verses that foretell the events. It came to Rossano in southern Italy, perhaps with Greek monks, and was rediscovered in the cathedral sacristy in 1879. It is listed in UNESCO's Memory of the World register and is a key work for the history of Christian book illustration.
image_caption: Rossano Gospels, folio 8v: Christ before Pilate

title: Rabbula Gospels
creator: early-christian-scribes
note: A Syriac Gospel book completed in 586 at a monastery in Mesopotamia, with one of the earliest images of the Crucifixion.
description: According to its colophon, this Syriac Gospel book was completed in 586 by the scribe Rabbula at the monastery of St John of Beth Zagba in northern Mesopotamia. Its decorated canon tables, which concord parallel passages of the four Gospels, are framed by arcades with birds, plants and small scenes, and several full-page miniatures show the Ascension, Pentecost and the Crucifixion, with Christ wearing a long purple robe between the two thieves. Some scholars think the full-page miniatures were added from another manuscript. It has been in Florence since the 15th century. It is an important witness both to Syriac Christianity, one of the great branches of the early church, and to the formation of Christian iconography later shared by East and West.
image_caption: Rabbula Gospels, folios 9v–10r, with decorated canon tables

title: Hexapla
creator: origen
location: Library of Caesarea (lost); fragments survive, e.g. in palimpsests in Milan and Cambridge
note: Origen's vast six-column edition of the Old Testament comparing the Hebrew text with Greek translations, the first great work of biblical textual criticism.
description: The Hexapla ('sixfold') set out the Old Testament in parallel columns: the Hebrew text, a Greek transliteration of the Hebrew, and the Greek versions of Aquila, Symmachus, the Septuagint and Theodotion, with extra columns for some books. In the Septuagint column Origen used critical signs borrowed from Alexandrian scholars of Homer to mark where the Greek had more or less than the Hebrew. The enormous work, perhaps some 6,000 leaves, was kept in the library at Caesarea, where Jerome consulted it, and was probably destroyed in the 7th century. Only fragments survive, in quotations, a Syriac translation of the Septuagint column and a few palimpsest leaves. It established a model for comparing biblical texts and shaped the Septuagint text used by later copyists.

title: On First Principles (De principiis)
creator: origen
location: Alexandria; survives mainly in Rufinus's Latin translation
note: The first systematic presentation of Christian theology, on God, creation, rational beings, free will and the interpretation of scripture.
description: Written in Alexandria, On First Principles sets out in four books what the church teaches clearly and explores more speculatively questions it leaves open: the Trinity, the creation of rational spirits, the fall, free will, the end of all things and how scripture should be read. Origen suggests that souls existed before bodies, that the material world was created as a place of education for fallen spirits, and that all might ultimately be restored to God, ideas that became controversial. His fourth book explains reading scripture according to body, soul and spirit, the literal, moral and spiritual senses. The Greek original was lost after Origen's condemnation in 553, and the main text is Rufinus's Latin translation of 398, which softened some passages, along with Greek fragments. The work set the pattern for later systematic theology.

title: On the Incarnation (De Incarnatione)
creator: athanasius
note: Athanasius's classic explanation of why the Word of God became human: to restore the image of God in humanity and defeat death.
description: On the Incarnation forms the second part of a two-part work, following Against the Gentiles. Athanasius argues that humanity, created in God's image through the Word, was falling back into corruption and nothingness through sin, and that only the Word himself, by becoming human, dying and rising, could renew that image and overcome death. He also argues from the spread of Christianity and the courage of martyrs that Christ is alive. Its date is debated, some placing it before the Arian controversy around 318 and others in the 330s. The phrase often summarised from it, that God became human so that humans might become divine, expresses the Eastern doctrine of deification. C. S. Lewis's introduction to a 1944 English translation helped make it widely read today.

title: Life of Antony
creator: athanasius
note: The biography of the Egyptian hermit Antony, the founding text of Christian monastic literature.
description: Written shortly after Antony's death in 356, the Life tells how the young Egyptian, hearing the Gospel command to sell all and give to the poor, gave away his property, lived as an ascetic near his village and then withdrew into the desert, first to an abandoned fort and later to the 'inner mountain' near the Red Sea. It describes his battles with demons, his counsel to visitors, his miracles and his support for Nicene orthodoxy. Translated into Latin within a few years, it spread the monastic ideal throughout the West. In his Confessions Augustine describes how hearing the story of Antony moved him on the eve of his conversion. Its scenes of temptation inspired painters from Bosch and Grünewald to Ernst and Dalí, and Flaubert's novel The Temptation of Saint Anthony.

title: Nicene Creed
creator: church-councils
note: The statement of faith in one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, shared by most Christian churches and recited in their liturgies.
description: The Council of Nicaea, summoned by the emperor Constantine in 325, adopted a creed declaring the Son 'of one substance' (homoousios) with the Father, against Arius, who held that the Son was created. The creed recited today in churches is usually the longer form associated with the Council of Constantinople in 381, which added fuller statements on the Holy Spirit, the church, baptism and resurrection; scholars debate exactly how this form arose. In the Latin West the words 'and the Son' (filioque) were later added to describe the Spirit's procession, beginning in Spain in the 6th century and adopted in Rome in the 11th; this became a lasting point of dispute with the Orthodox churches. The creed is used by Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and many other churches and has been set to music in countless masses as the Credo.
image_caption: Icon of the First Council of Nicaea, with the creed

title: Chalcedonian Definition
creator: church-councils
note: The council's statement that Christ is one person in two natures, divine and human, 'without confusion, without change, without division, without separation'.
description: The Council of Chalcedon was called by the emperor Marcian in 451, after decades of conflict over how Christ is both God and man. Drawing on Cyril of Alexandria and on the Tome of Pope Leo I, it declared Christ to be one person 'acknowledged in two natures', fully divine and fully human. The definition became the standard of orthodoxy for the Greek and Latin churches and later for most Protestant churches. It was rejected by many Christians in Egypt, Syria and Armenia, who held to 'one nature' formulas; their churches, today called Oriental Orthodox (such as the Coptic, Syriac, Armenian and Ethiopian churches), separated from Constantinople and Rome. In recent decades theologians from both sides have agreed that the dispute was largely about terminology.

title: On the Holy Spirit
creator: basil-of-caesarea
note: Basil's defence of the full divinity of the Holy Spirit, which prepared for the creed of Constantinople in 381.
description: Basil wrote On the Holy Spirit after being criticised for using a doxology that glorified the Father 'with the Son, together with the Holy Spirit', implying their equality. Against the Pneumatomachi ('Spirit-fighters'), who denied the Spirit's divinity, he argues from scripture, from the baptismal formula and from the church's unwritten tradition of worship that the Spirit is to be honoured together with the Father and the Son. He is careful not to call the Spirit 'God' directly, a caution that reflects the politics of the time. The treatise was a major influence on the Council of Constantinople and on all later Trinitarian theology, and is also an early witness to the idea of authoritative unwritten tradition.

title: Asketikon (Rules of St Basil)
creator: basil-of-caesarea
note: The question-and-answer rules that Basil wrote for monastic communities, still the basis of Orthodox monastic life.
description: Basil's Asketikon developed in several editions from his visits to monks and his own community in Pontus. Its 'Longer Rules' and 'Shorter Rules' answer questions about Christian life in community: obedience, prayer, work, poverty, the care of children, and how to live with others in love. Basil favoured cenobitic, communal monasticism over solitary hermit life, asking how a hermit could wash anyone's feet. He also expected monasteries to serve their neighbours, an ideal realised in his hospital complex at Caesarea. A Latin version by Rufinus influenced Benedict of Nursia, who recommends 'the Rule of our holy father Basil' in his own Rule. In the Orthodox world, monks are often described as following the tradition of St Basil.

title: Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom
creator: john-chrysostom
location: Constantinople; celebrated in Orthodox and Eastern Catholic churches
note: The eucharistic service most often celebrated in the Orthodox Church, traditionally ascribed to Chrysostom.
description: The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom is the standard eucharistic service of the Byzantine rite, used on most Sundays and weekdays in Orthodox and Eastern Catholic churches; the longer Liturgy of St Basil is used on certain feasts. Its central prayer, the anaphora, may go back to Chrysostom's time in Antioch or Constantinople, and scholars think he may have adapted an earlier anaphora; much of the rest of the service grew around it over the following centuries in the imperial capital. It includes litanies, the Little and Great Entrances, the Cherubic Hymn, the Creed, the consecration and communion. It has been translated into many languages and set to music by composers such as Tchaikovsky and Rachmaninoff.

title: On the Priesthood
creator: john-chrysostom
note: A dialogue on the dignity and dangers of the priestly office, one of the most widely read works of the Greek Fathers.
description: In six books, Chrysostom imagines a conversation with his friend Basil (not Basil of Caesarea), whom he had tricked into accepting ordination while himself avoiding it. Justifying his evasion, he describes the awesome responsibility of the priest, who offers the eucharist and must guide souls, and the qualities a priest needs: wisdom, patience, eloquence, and resistance to vanity and to the pressures of powerful laypeople. It is a classic of pastoral literature, much read in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance, and a source for the high view of priesthood in both Eastern and Western churches.

title: Vulgate
creator: jerome
location: Rome and Bethlehem; standard text of the Latin Church
note: Jerome's Latin translation of the Bible, which became the standard Bible of the Western church for over a thousand years.
description: In 382 Pope Damasus asked Jerome to revise the existing Old Latin versions of the Gospels, which varied widely. Jerome went further: in Bethlehem he translated most of the Old Testament directly from the Hebrew between about 390 and 405, an innovation that some, including Augustine, at first opposed. The other New Testament books in the Vulgate were revised by other, unknown scholars, and some books, such as the Psalms in their liturgical form, came from his earlier revisions based on the Greek. The resulting collection, later called the versio vulgata, 'common version', gradually displaced other Latin texts, and the Carolingians produced careful editions. The Council of Trent declared it authentic in 1546, and an official edition, the Sixto-Clementine Vulgate, followed in 1592. Its Latin shaped the language of the liturgy, theology, and much medieval European literature and art.
image_caption: Vulgate manuscript, Stiftsbibliothek St Gallen, Cod. Sang. 63

title: Confessions
creator: augustine
note: Augustine's account of his restless life and conversion, addressed as a prayer to God, the first great Western autobiography.
description: In thirteen books addressed to God, Augustine recounts his childhood in Thagaste, including the theft of pears that he analyses as a sin done for its own sake, his studies in Carthage, his years as a Manichaean and a teacher of rhetoric, and his mother Monica's prayers. In Milan, influenced by Neoplatonism and by Ambrose, he struggles with his attachment to sexual desire and worldly success until, in a garden in 386, he hears a child's voice say 'take up and read', opens Paul's letters and is converted. After describing his mother's death, he turns to meditations on memory, time and the creation story in Genesis. The book's famous opening declares that the human heart is restless until it rests in God. The Confessions profoundly influenced Christian spirituality and the Western tradition of self-examination, from Petrarch to Rousseau and modern autobiography.
image_caption: Augustine's Confessions in a manuscript

title: The City of God
creator: augustine
note: Augustine's vast response to the sack of Rome, contrasting the earthly city of self-love with the heavenly city of the love of God.
description: When the Visigoths sacked Rome in 410, pagans blamed the disaster on the abandonment of the old gods. In twenty-two books written over thirteen years, Augustine first argues that the gods had never protected Rome and that pagan religion and philosophy cannot give true happiness, then traces through history two 'cities', defined by two loves: the earthly city of self-love, and the city of God, a community of the faithful on pilgrimage through this world toward its fulfilment beyond history. Along the way he discusses creation, the fall, the Roman Empire, providence, peace and the last things. The work shaped medieval ideas of church and state and Western philosophies of history, and it was one of the most copied books of the Middle Ages.
image_caption: A medieval illuminated manuscript of The City of God

title: On the Trinity (De Trinitate)
creator: augustine
note: Augustine's fifteen-book study of the doctrine of the Trinity, seeking its image in the human mind's memory, understanding and will.
description: Augustine worked on On the Trinity for some twenty years. The first books set out the scriptural basis and the vocabulary of the doctrine of one God in three persons, defending the equality of the Son and Spirit with the Father. The later books turn inward, looking for analogies of the Trinity in the human mind, made in God's image, most famously the triad of memory, understanding and will. The work became the foundation of Latin Trinitarian theology; its account of the Spirit as the love between Father and Son underlies the Western filioque. Medieval theologians from Anselm to Aquinas built on it.

title: The Mystical Theology
creator: pseudo-dionysius
note: A brief, influential treatise teaching that God is known by unknowing, beyond all affirmation and negation.
description: Only five short chapters long, The Mystical Theology begins with a prayer to the Trinity to lead the soul 'beyond unknowing' into the 'brilliant darkness' of a hidden silence. Using the image of Moses ascending Mount Sinai into the cloud, it teaches that the soul must leave behind sense and intellect to be united with God, who transcends every name, and that negations of what God is not are truer than affirmations. Accepted for a thousand years as the work of Paul's convert, it carried near-apostolic authority. Through the Latin translations of Eriugena and others it shaped medieval mysticism, including Bonaventure, Eckhart and the anonymous English Cloud of Unknowing, and Orthodox theology through Maximus the Confessor and Gregory Palamas.

title: The Celestial Hierarchy
creator: pseudo-dionysius
note: The source of the classic medieval ordering of the angels into nine choirs in three hierarchies.
description: The Celestial Hierarchy explains the biblical names of heavenly beings by arranging them into three ranks of three: seraphim, cherubim and thrones; dominions, powers and authorities; principalities, archangels and angels. Each rank receives divine illumination from the one above and passes it on below, so that the whole hierarchy draws creatures back toward God. Its companion, The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, describes the church's sacraments and orders as reflecting the heavenly ones. The scheme was taken up by Gregory the Great, Aquinas and Dante, whose Paradiso follows it, and it shaped medieval art and ideas of order in church and society. Abbot Suger's Gothic rebuilding of Saint-Denis has often been linked to its theology of light, though the extent of that influence is debated.

title: Rule of Saint Benedict
creator: benedict
location: Monte Cassino; oldest surviving copy (c. 700) in the Bodleian Library, Oxford (MS Hatton 48)
note: Benedict's guide for monastic life, balancing prayer, work and study, the foundation of Western monasticism.
description: The Rule, in a prologue and seventy-three short chapters, sets out how a community of monks should live under an abbot. It orders the day around the Divine Office, the eight services of communal prayer in which the Psalms are sung each week, alternating with manual labour and lectio divina, the slow prayerful reading of scripture. It covers obedience, silence and humility, which it describes as a ladder of twelve steps, as well as food, sleep, clothing, the reception of guests 'as Christ', discipline and the election of the abbot. Benedict drew on earlier rules, especially the anonymous Rule of the Master, but his is notably moderate, calling itself 'a little rule for beginners'. Promoted by Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, it became the norm for Western monasteries, and is still followed by Benedictines, Cistercians and Trappists. The oldest surviving copy, written in England around 700, is in the Bodleian Library in Oxford, while a 9th-century manuscript at St Gallen preserves the text most faithfully.
image_caption: The oldest surviving copy of the Rule, c. 700, Bodleian Library, Oxford (MS Hatton 48)

title: Pastoral Rule (Regula pastoralis)
creator: gregory-the-great
note: Gregory's guide for bishops on the qualities of a pastor and how to counsel different kinds of people.
description: Written at the start of his pontificate, the Pastoral Rule explains who should accept the office of shepherd of souls, how a pastor should live, and above all how to adapt teaching to different listeners: the poor and the rich, the joyful and the sad, the proud and the timid, the married and the celibate, and so on through some forty contrasting pairs. It closes by warning the pastor against pride in his own success. The book was sent to bishops throughout the West; Alfred the Great translated it into Old English in the 890s, with a preface lamenting the decline of learning, and Byzantine emperors had it translated into Greek. It shaped the ideal of the bishop throughout the Middle Ages.

title: Dialogues
creator: gregory-the-great
note: Four books of stories of Italian holy men, including the only early life of Benedict of Nursia.
description: Framed as conversations between Gregory and his deacon Peter, the Dialogues collect miracle stories of holy men of 6th-century Italy, to show that sanctity had not disappeared from Italy in an age of war and plague. The second book is devoted entirely to Benedict and is the main source for his life. The fourth book discusses the fate of souls after death, with visions that contributed to the development of the Western doctrine of purgatory. A minority of scholars has argued that the Dialogues were not written by Gregory, but most accept them as his. They were immensely popular, translated into Greek by Pope Zacharias and into Old English at Alfred's court.

title: Book of Kells
creator: insular-scribes
note: The most lavish of the Insular Gospel books, a masterpiece of interlace, spirals and fantastical animals.
description: The Book of Kells contains the four Gospels in Latin, on 340 surviving vellum leaves. It was probably begun in the monastery of Iona, off the west coast of Scotland, around 800 and taken to Kells in Ireland after Viking raids, though where each part was made is debated. Its decoration is extraordinary: full-page portraits of Christ, the Virgin and Child and the evangelists, symbols of the four evangelists, and dense carpet-like pages of knotwork and spirals, most famously the Chi-Rho page, where the monogram of Christ's name swells to fill the page, with cats, mice and otters hidden in its ornament. Even ordinary text pages are enlivened with animals and figures. The manuscript, recorded at Kells in the 11th century, was stolen in 1007 and its gold cover lost. It came to Trinity College Dublin in the 17th century, where it is displayed, a page turned regularly.
image_caption: Book of Kells, folio 32v: Christ enthroned

title: Lindisfarne Gospels
creator: insular-scribes
note: A Northumbrian Gospel book of the early 8th century, with a later Old English gloss that is the oldest surviving English version of the Gospels.
description: The Lindisfarne Gospels was made at the monastery of Lindisfarne, on Holy Island off the Northumbrian coast, probably in honour of St Cuthbert. A colophon added in the 10th century by the priest Aldred names Eadfrith, bishop of Lindisfarne from 698 to 721, as its scribe and artist, and most scholars accept that one person wrote and illuminated it. Each Gospel is preceded by an evangelist portrait, based on Mediterranean models, and a 'carpet page' of intricate interlace in the form of a cross, followed by a decorated initial page. Its pigments were made from local and imported materials. Aldred added a word-by-word translation into the Northumbrian dialect of Old English between the lines. The book was taken to Durham, then confiscated at the dissolution of the monasteries, and entered the British Library's collections through the library of Sir Robert Cotton.
image_caption: Lindisfarne Gospels, folio 27r: the opening of Matthew's Gospel

title: Book of Durrow
creator: insular-scribes
note: The earliest surviving fully decorated Insular Gospel book, with bold carpet pages and evangelist symbols.
description: The Book of Durrow is a small Gospel book in Latin, written in Insular majuscule and decorated with six carpet pages, symbols of the evangelists and decorated initials, in a limited palette of yellow, red, green and brown. Its ornament combines Celtic trumpet spirals, Germanic animal interlace like that on the Sutton Hoo metalwork, and Mediterranean motifs. It was kept at the monastery of Durrow in Ireland, founded by St Columba, but scholars debate whether it was made there, at Iona or in Northumbria. In the 17th century it was reportedly dipped in water by a farmer to cure sick cattle. It is the earliest of the great series that culminates in the Book of Kells.
image_caption: Book of Durrow, folio 86r (Trinity College Dublin, MS 57)

title: Codex Amiatinus
creator: insular-scribes
note: The oldest surviving complete Latin Vulgate Bible, made at Wearmouth-Jarrow in Northumbria as a gift for the pope.
description: Codex Amiatinus is a giant single-volume Bible of over a thousand leaves, weighing more than 34 kilograms, one of three such pandects made at the twin monastery of Wearmouth-Jarrow under Abbot Ceolfrith, Bede's abbot. In 716 Ceolfrith set out to carry it to Rome as a gift for the pope but died on the way at Langres. The manuscript later reached the abbey of San Salvatore on Monte Amiata in Tuscany, from which it takes its name; its Northumbrian origin was recognised only in the 1880s, when a dedication altered to disguise its origin was deciphered. Written in a fine Italian-style uncial, it includes a famous image of the prophet Ezra writing at a book cupboard. It is the most important witness to the text of Jerome's Vulgate.
image_caption: Codex Amiatinus, folio 5r: the prophet Ezra writing

title: Ecclesiastical History of the English People
creator: bede
location: Jarrow, Northumbria; early manuscripts include the St Petersburg Bede and the Moore Bede
note: Bede's history of the conversion of the English to Christianity, the foundation of English history.
description: Completed in 731, Bede's Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum tells, in five books, the story of Britain from the Roman invasion to his own day, centred on the conversion of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms through Pope Gregory's mission to Kent in 597 and the Irish mission from Iona to Northumbria. It records the Synod of Whitby of 664, the lives of saints such as Aidan and Cuthbert, the cowherd poet Cædmon and many miracles. Bede named his sources and used documents obtained from Canterbury and Rome, and he dated events by the year of the Lord, popularising AD dating. Historians value it highly while noting its Northumbrian and Roman sympathies. It survives in over 150 manuscripts and was translated into Old English in the reign of Alfred.
image_caption: The St Petersburg Bede, 8th century, folio 3v

title: Mishnah
creator: judah-ha-nasi
location: Galilee; earliest complete manuscript, the Kaufmann Codex, in Budapest
note: The first written compilation of the Jewish oral law, organised in six orders, and the foundation of the Talmud.
description: The Mishnah collects the legal teachings of the rabbis known as Tannaim, from roughly the 1st century BC to about 200 AD, edited according to tradition by Judah ha-Nasi. Written in a concise Hebrew, it is arranged in six orders covering agriculture and blessings, Sabbath and festivals, women and marriage, damages and civil law, holy things and sacrifices, and purity, divided into sixty-three tractates. It often records disagreements between named sages, such as the houses of Hillel and Shammai, alongside anonymous rulings. Remarkably, much of it discusses Temple rituals that could no longer be performed, showing how the rabbis preserved and reinterpreted the tradition. The tractate Avot, 'Sayings of the Fathers', is a widely loved collection of ethical maxims. The Mishnah became the basis of both Talmuds and of the study of Jewish law ever since.
image_caption: The Kaufmann manuscript of the Mishnah (MS Kaufmann A 50), Budapest

title: Jerusalem Talmud
creator: talmud-sages
location: Tiberias and Sepphoris, Galilee; only complete manuscript, Leiden University Library
note: The commentary on the Mishnah compiled in the academies of Galilee, also called the Talmud of the Land of Israel.
description: Despite its name, the Jerusalem Talmud (Talmud Yerushalmi) was compiled in Galilee, chiefly in Tiberias, in the late 4th century, when Jews were barred from Jerusalem. It records the discussions of the Amoraim of the Land of Israel on the Mishnah, in Western Aramaic and Hebrew, covering the first four orders and part of the sixth. It is especially important for laws connected with agriculture in the land of Israel. Its editing appears hurried and incomplete, perhaps because of political pressures in the late Roman period. Less studied than the Babylonian Talmud, it has been the subject of renewed scholarly attention. The only complete manuscript, copied in 1289, is in Leiden, and the first printed edition was published by Daniel Bomberg in Venice in 1523–24.
image_caption: A page of the Jerusalem Talmud

title: Babylonian Talmud
creator: talmud-sages
location: Academies of Babylonia (Sura and Pumbedita); oldest complete manuscript, Munich, 1342
note: The vast record of rabbinic discussion on the Mishnah compiled in Babylonia, the central text of Jewish learning for fifteen centuries.
description: The Babylonian Talmud (Talmud Bavli) consists of the Mishnah together with the Gemara, the discussions of generations of Babylonian rabbis, in Aramaic and Hebrew, on thirty-seven of its tractates. Its debates move associatively from legal questions to biblical interpretation, ethics, medicine, folklore and stories of the sages, preserving minority opinions as well as rulings. Scholars debate how and when it took final shape; anonymous later editors are now thought to have shaped much of its argumentative structure. Through the Geonim of Babylonia it became authoritative throughout the Jewish world. The 1520–23 Venice edition of Daniel Bomberg fixed its page layout, with Rashi's commentary and the Tosafot around the text, and the famous Vilna edition of the 1880s standardised it further. Copies were burned in Paris in 1242 and elsewhere after Christian condemnations. Its study, in yeshivas and today in the worldwide daily-page cycle, is at the heart of Jewish religious culture.

image_caption: Pages from 16th-century printed Talmud editions by Daniel Bomberg and Ambrosius Froben

title: Midrash Rabbah
creator: talmud-sages
location: Land of Israel and elsewhere; first printed Constantinople and Venice, 16th century
note: The 'Great Midrash': rabbinic collections of interpretation, stories and sermons on the Torah and the five Megillot.
description: Midrash is the rabbinic art of interpreting scripture, filling gaps in the biblical narrative, drawing out laws and morals, and linking distant verses. Midrash Rabbah is a set of ten collections on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy and on the Song of Songs, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes and Esther. They were compiled at very different times: Genesis Rabbah and Leviticus Rabbah in the Land of Israel around the 5th century, others as late as the 12th. They were grouped together only in the printed editions of the 16th century. Their parables and stories, such as Abraham smashing his father's idols, became a common heritage of Jewish teaching and preaching.

title: On the Divine Images
creator: john-of-damascus
note: Three treatises defending the veneration of icons against Byzantine iconoclasm, the classic Orthodox theology of images.
description: When Emperor Leo III moved against religious images, John, writing under Muslim rule beyond the emperor's reach, composed three apologies for icons. He argues that while the invisible God cannot be depicted, God became visible in Christ, so that to refuse images of Christ is to deny the reality of the incarnation. He distinguishes worship (latreia), due only to God, from veneration (proskynesis) given to icons, and notes that honour paid to an image passes to its prototype. He gathers quotations from scripture and the Fathers in support. His arguments shaped the decrees of the Second Council of Nicaea in 787, which restored icon veneration, and remain the foundation of Orthodox iconography.

title: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith
creator: john-of-damascus
note: A summary of Greek patristic doctrine that became the standard textbook of Orthodox theology and influenced Western scholasticism.
description: The Exposition forms the third part of John's Fount of Knowledge, after a section on philosophy and one on heresies, including a chapter on Islam that is among the earliest Christian discussions of it. In a hundred chapters, it gathers the teachings of the Greek Fathers, above all the Cappadocians and Maximus the Confessor, on God, the Trinity, creation, angels, humanity, Christ, the sacraments, icons and the last things. Translated into Latin by Burgundio of Pisa around 1150, it was used by Peter Lombard and Thomas Aquinas, making John an important link between Eastern and Western theology.

title: Christ Pantocrator of Sinai
creator: byzantine-iconographers
location: St Catherine's Monastery, Mount Sinai, Egypt
note: One of the oldest surviving icons of Christ, painted in wax, which survived iconoclasm in the remote Sinai monastery.
description: This icon, about 84 centimetres high, shows Christ as Pantocrator, 'ruler of all', holding a jewelled Gospel book and raising his right hand in blessing. It was painted in encaustic, pigment mixed with hot wax, a technique inherited from Roman Egyptian portraiture, probably in Constantinople in the 6th century and perhaps donated by the emperor Justinian, who founded the monastery. The two sides of Christ's face differ noticeably, which has been interpreted as expressing his two natures, divine and human. Because St Catherine's lay outside the Byzantine Empire during iconoclasm, its icons escaped the destruction of images, and this one, rediscovered under later overpainting in the 1960s, is the model for the Pantocrator image found in countless later icons and church domes.
image_caption: Christ Pantocrator, 6th century, St Catherine's Monastery, Sinai

title: Theotokos of Vladimir
creator: byzantine-iconographers
location: State Tretyakov Gallery (Church of St Nicholas in Tolmachi), Moscow
note: A Byzantine icon of the Virgin tenderly embracing the Christ Child, the most venerated icon of Russia.
description: Painted in Constantinople around 1130, this icon was sent to Kievan Rus' and taken in 1155 by Prince Andrei Bogolyubsky to Vladimir, where it gave the icon its name. It shows the Virgin and Child cheek to cheek, a type called Eleousa ('tenderness' or 'mercy'), with Mary's sorrowful gaze seeming to foresee the Passion. Only the faces are original; the rest was repainted over the centuries. Brought to Moscow in 1395, it was credited with protecting the city from Tamerlane and other invaders and became a national palladium, used at coronations. After the Revolution it entered the Tretyakov Gallery and is today displayed in the gallery's church so that it may be both seen and venerated. It is regarded as one of the masterpieces of Byzantine painting.
image_caption: The Theotokos of Vladimir, c. 1130 (Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow)

title: Deësis mosaic, Hagia Sophia
creator: byzantine-iconographers
note: Christ flanked by the Virgin Mary and John the Baptist interceding for humanity, a masterpiece of late Byzantine art.
description: The Deësis ('supplication') mosaic in the south gallery of Hagia Sophia shows Christ in majesty between the Virgin and John the Baptist, who turn toward him in prayer on behalf of humankind. It is usually dated to around 1261, after Byzantine forces recovered Constantinople from the Latin crusaders, though some scholars have suggested other dates. The faces are modelled with exceptionally fine tesserae and subtle gradations of colour, giving them a softness and humanity that anticipate developments in Italian painting. Much of the lower part has been lost. After 1453 Hagia Sophia became a mosque and the mosaics were covered; they were uncovered and restored in the 1930s, when the building became a museum, and remain visible in the gallery.
image_caption: The Deësis mosaic in the south gallery of Hagia Sophia, Istanbul

title: Trinity
creator: rublev
note: Three angels seated at a table, representing the Holy Trinity, the most celebrated of all Russian icons.
description: The icon depicts the three angels who visited Abraham at Mamre (Genesis 18), a scene traditionally read by Christians as a revelation of the Trinity. Rublev left out Abraham and Sarah, who usually appear, and concentrated on the three figures seated around a table bearing a chalice, their heads inclined toward each other in a circle of silent communion. Behind them are a house, a tree and a mountain. The soft blues, greens and golds and the balance of the composition have made it a symbol of harmony and peace. Painted for the Trinity monastery of St Sergius, perhaps in his memory, it was transferred to the Tretyakov Gallery in 1929. The Russian Church council of 1551 held it up as a model for representing the Trinity.
image_file: Andrey Rublev - Св. Троица - Google Art Project.jpg
image_caption: Andrei Rublev, Trinity (Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow)

title: Commentary on the Torah
creator: rashi
location: Troyes, Champagne; first dated Hebrew printed book, Reggio di Calabria, 1475
note: Rashi's line-by-line commentary on the Five Books of Moses, the most studied Jewish commentary on the Bible.
description: Rashi explains the Torah phrase by phrase, clarifying difficult words, grammar and context and answering questions a careful reader would raise, while weaving in selected rabbinic midrash where it helps the plain sense. His comments are brief and clear, and he occasionally translates a word into Old French, written in Hebrew letters. The commentary became the standard companion to the Torah text, studied by children and scholars alike; the custom of studying 'Chumash with Rashi' persists. It has generated hundreds of super-commentaries. Printed in Reggio di Calabria in 1475, it was the first dated Hebrew book. In Latin translation and through Nicholas of Lyra, it influenced Christian exegesis and the Reformation Bibles.

title: Commentary on the Talmud
creator: rashi
location: Troyes, Champagne; printed in the inner margin of every standard Talmud edition
note: The indispensable running commentary that makes the Babylonian Talmud readable, printed beside its text since 1520.
description: Rashi's commentary on the Babylonian Talmud explains the flow of the argument, defines terms, supplies the background and identifies speakers, enabling students without a teacher to follow the dense Aramaic discussions. It covers most of the tractates; for a few, the commentary was completed by his students and grandsons. Since Daniel Bomberg's Venice edition of 1520–23, it has been printed in the inner column of every standard Talmud page, opposite the Tosafot, the critical glosses of Rashi's successors. Its distinctive semi-cursive script, used for commentaries, is called 'Rashi script'. It is essential to traditional Talmud study.

title: Proslogion
creator: anselm
note: Anselm's prayerful meditation containing the 'ontological argument' that God is that than which nothing greater can be conceived.
description: Written at Bec as a sequel to his Monologion, the Proslogion ('address') takes the form of a prayer seeking to understand what is believed, 'faith seeking understanding'. In its second chapter Anselm argues that God is 'something than which nothing greater can be thought'; since what exists in reality as well as in the mind is greater than what exists in the mind alone, such a being must exist. The monk Gaunilo replied that the same reasoning could prove the existence of a perfect island, and Anselm answered him; both texts circulated together. The argument was rejected by Aquinas, revived in different forms by Descartes and Leibniz, criticised by Kant, and is still debated by philosophers of religion.

title: Cur Deus Homo (Why God Became Man)
creator: anselm
note: A dialogue explaining the incarnation and crucifixion as the satisfaction of humanity's debt to God's honour.
description: In this dialogue with his pupil Boso, Anselm argues 'leaving Christ out of view' that human sin dishonours God and requires satisfaction greater than anything humans can give, yet owed by humans; only one who is both God and man can make it, and Christ's freely offered death does so. The book rejected the older idea that Christ's death paid a ransom to the devil. Its 'satisfaction theory' strongly influenced medieval and Reformation teaching on atonement, including later theories of penal substitution, and has also been criticised, by Abelard in his own time and by modern theologians, for emphasising justice over love.

title: Sermons on the Song of Songs
creator: bernard-of-clairvaux
note: Eighty-six sermons on the first two chapters of the Song of Songs, a summit of medieval mystical writing about the love between God and the soul.
description: Bernard began these sermons for his monks in 1135 and was still writing them at his death, having reached only the beginning of the third chapter of the Song. Using the poem's language of kisses, longing and union, he describes the soul as the bride of Christ, the Word, and traces the stages of its love, from repentance to contemplation. The sermons were polished literary compositions rather than transcripts, written in rich, rhythmic Latin full of scriptural echoes. They became a major source for later bridal mysticism, including the women mystics of the 13th century, and for devotional language in Catholicism and, through Luther and Calvin who admired Bernard, in Protestantism.

title: On Loving God (De diligendo Deo)
creator: bernard-of-clairvaux
note: A short treatise explaining why and how God is to be loved, describing four degrees of love.
description: Asked by Cardinal Haimeric why and how God should be loved, Bernard replies that the reason for loving God is God himself, and the measure is to love without measure. He describes four degrees of love: loving oneself for one's own sake, loving God for one's own sake, loving God for God's sake, and finally loving oneself only for God's sake, a state rarely reached in this life. The treatise is one of the most accessible and widely read works of medieval spirituality.

title: Scivias
creator: hildegard
location: Disibodenberg and Rupertsberg; the illuminated Rupertsberg manuscript survives in a 20th-century facsimile
note: Hildegard's first visionary work, twenty-six visions of creation, redemption and the church, with striking illuminations.
description: Scivias, short for Scito vias Domini, 'Know the ways of the Lord', records twenty-six visions in three books, each described and then explained by a heavenly voice: the first on creation and the fall, the second on redemption through Christ and the sacraments, and the third on the history of salvation and the end of the world, ending with songs of praise. Hildegard says she saw these things not in dreams or ecstasy but awake, in a 'living light'. Pope Eugenius III read part of it at the Synod of Trier in 1147–48 and encouraged her to continue. A splendid illuminated manuscript made at Rupertsberg, perhaps under her direction, was lost from Dresden in the Second World War, but survives in a hand-painted facsimile made by nuns of Eibingen in the 1920s.
image_caption: Hildegard receiving a vision, from the Rupertsberg Scivias manuscript

title: Book of Divine Works (Liber Divinorum Operum)
creator: hildegard
location: Rupertsberg; illuminated manuscript in the Biblioteca Statale, Lucca
note: Hildegard's last and most ambitious visionary work, showing the human being at the centre of the cosmos.
description: In ten visions Hildegard sets out a theology of creation in which the universe, with its winds, elements and heavenly bodies, is held in the embrace of divine love, and the human being, made of the same elements, is a microcosm of the whole. She also interprets the opening of John's Gospel and the history of salvation. The famous illuminated manuscript of the early 13th century in Lucca shows a cosmic figure embracing the circles of the universe, with a human figure at its centre. The work reflects Hildegard's interest in medicine and nature and has been much admired in modern times for its integrated vision of humanity and creation.
image_file: Hildegard von Bingen Liber Divinorum Operum.jpg
image_caption: Cosmic figure from the Lucca manuscript of the Liber Divinorum Operum

title: Four Books of Sentences
creator: peter-lombard
note: An organised collection of patristic teaching on all of Christian doctrine, the standard textbook of medieval theology.
description: The Sentences arranges quotations, mainly from Augustine but also from other Fathers, under four headings: God and the Trinity; creation and sin; the incarnation and the virtues; and the sacraments and the last things. Where authorities seem to disagree, Peter offers his own resolutions. After the Fourth Lateran Council endorsed his teaching on the Trinity in 1215, the Sentences became the core of the theology curriculum: Alexander of Hales introduced lectures on it at Paris in the 1220s, and commenting on it became a stage in every theologian's career. Thousands of commentaries survive, and it was only displaced by Aquinas's Summa in the 16th century.

image_caption: Medieval manuscript leaf, Free Library of Philadelphia, Lewis E 170

title: Commentary on the Mishnah (with the Thirteen Principles)
creator: maimonides
location: Written in Morocco and Egypt in Judeo-Arabic; autograph portions in the Bodleian Library, Oxford
note: Maimonides's first major work, a commentary on the whole Mishnah containing his Thirteen Principles of Jewish faith.
description: Begun when Maimonides was twenty-three and completed in Egypt in 1168, the commentary, written in Arabic in Hebrew characters, explains every tractate of the Mishnah and summarises the conclusions of the Talmud. Its introductions became famous in their own right: the 'Eight Chapters' on ethics, preceding the tractate Avot, and the introduction to the chapter Helek of tractate Sanhedrin, where Maimonides sets out thirteen principles of faith, including God's existence, unity and incorporeality, the prophecy of Moses, the divine origin of the Torah, reward and punishment, the coming of the Messiah and the resurrection of the dead. The principles were debated by later Jewish thinkers, but versified as the hymn Yigdal and as the 'Ani Ma'amin' creed they entered the prayer book. Parts of Maimonides's autograph manuscript survive in Oxford.

title: Mishneh Torah
creator: maimonides
location: Fustat, Egypt; illuminated manuscripts include the Kaufmann Mishneh Torah in Budapest
note: Maimonides's fourteen-book code of the whole of Jewish law, organised by subject in clear Hebrew.
description: In the Mishneh Torah ('Repetition of the Torah') Maimonides set out to summarise all of Jewish law, including laws no longer practised such as those of the Temple and the king, so that anyone could know the law without wading through the Talmud. He organised it in fourteen books, from the fundamentals of faith and knowledge of God to the laws of kings and the Messiah, in a lucid Mishnaic Hebrew, usually without citing sources or recording debates. That omission provoked criticism, notably from Rabbi Abraham ben David of Posquières, whose critical glosses are printed with it, and fears that it would replace Talmud study. It became one of the pillars of Jewish law, together with the later Shulchan Aruch of Joseph Karo. Fine illuminated copies were made in medieval Spain, Italy and Germany.

title: Guide for the Perplexed
creator: maimonides
location: Fustat, Egypt; written in Judeo-Arabic, translated into Hebrew by Samuel ibn Tibbon
note: Maimonides's philosophical masterpiece, reconciling the Torah with Aristotelian philosophy for readers torn between them.
description: Addressed to a student perplexed by apparent conflicts between scripture and philosophy, the Guide interprets the Bible's anthropomorphic language about God figuratively, argues that God can only be described by negations, discusses whether the world is eternal or created (favouring creation while admitting it cannot be proven), and explains prophecy, providence, evil and the reasons for the commandments. Maimonides warned that he wrote it deliberately obscurely in places, and readers have long debated its true teaching. Its rationalism provoked fierce controversy in the 13th century, with copies burned in Montpellier in 1232. In Latin translation it influenced Aquinas and other scholastics, and later Spinoza and Leibniz.
