image_caption: Manuscript page in Maimonides's hand, Arabic written in Hebrew letters

title: Kuzari
creator: judah-halevi
location: Spain; written in Judeo-Arabic, translated into Hebrew by Judah ibn Tibbon in 1167
note: A dialogue in which the king of the Khazars questions a philosopher, a Christian, a Muslim and a rabbi, and chooses Judaism.
description: The Kuzari is built on the historical tradition that the ruling class of the Khazars, a Turkic people of the Caucasus steppes, converted to Judaism in the 8th or 9th century. In Halevi's book the king, told in a dream that his intentions are pleasing to God but not his actions, interviews a philosopher, a Christian scholar and a Muslim scholar before turning to a rabbi. The rabbi grounds his faith not in philosophical proofs but in God's revelation in history, witnessed publicly by the whole people at Sinai, and speaks of the special religious capacity of Israel and the holiness of the Land of Israel. The book closes with the rabbi's decision to go to Jerusalem, as Halevi himself did. It has remained a classic of Jewish thought.
image_caption: A page of the Kuzari, Warsaw edition, 1880

title: Zohar
creator: moses-de-leon
location: Castile; first printed in Mantua and Cremona, 1558–60
note: The foundational work of Kabbalah, a mystical commentary on the Torah in Aramaic, set among the sages of 2nd-century Galilee.
description: The Zohar ('Radiance') is a vast collection of mystical interpretations of the Torah, the Song of Songs, Ruth and other texts, written in an artificial literary Aramaic. Its stories portray Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and his companions wandering through Galilee, discussing the hidden meanings of scripture. It develops the kabbalistic doctrine of the ten sefirot, the aspects through which the hidden God (Ein Sof) is manifest, and speaks of the divine feminine presence, the Shekhinah, of exile and redemption, and of how human deeds affect the divine realm. Tradition attributes it to bar Yochai. Most scholars since Gershom Scholem date it to late 13th-century Castile and link it to Moses de León, some seeing it as the work of a circle of kabbalists composed over time. It became a sacred text for many Jews, central to the Kabbalah of Safed and to Hasidism.
image_caption: An early printed edition of the Zohar

title: Canticle of the Sun
creator: francis-of-assisi
location: San Damiano, Assisi; earliest text in Assisi, Biblioteca del Sacro Convento, Cod. 338
note: Francis's hymn praising God through 'Brother Sun', 'Sister Moon', wind, water, fire, earth and 'Sister Death'.
description: According to early sources, Francis composed the Canticle of the Creatures, also called the Canticle of Brother Sun, in 1225 while ill and nearly blind at San Damiano. In Umbrian Italian rather than Latin, it praises the Lord 'through' (or 'for', the Italian per being ambiguous) Brother Sun, Sister Moon and the stars, Brothers Wind and Fire, Sister Water and Mother Earth. Francis later added a stanza on pardon and peace, reportedly to reconcile the bishop and mayor of Assisi, and a final one welcoming Sister Bodily Death. It is among the earliest literary works in Italian. Its vision of creation as a family has made it one of the best-loved Christian texts, and Pope Francis took its opening words, Laudato si', as the title of his 2015 encyclical on the environment.

title: Rule of St Francis (Regula bullata)
creator: francis-of-assisi
location: Approved by Pope Honorius III; papal bull preserved in the Sacro Convento, Assisi
note: The final rule of the Franciscan friars, approved by the pope in 1223, centred on poverty, humility and preaching.
description: Francis's first, very simple rule of about 1209 consisted mainly of Gospel passages; a longer 'Rule without a bull' followed in 1221. The definitive rule, approved by Honorius III's bull Solet annuere in November 1223, is shorter and more juridical, prescribing that the friars 'observe the holy Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, living in obedience, without anything of their own, and in chastity'. Friars were to own nothing, not to receive money, to work or beg, and to preach briefly. How strictly to keep this poverty became a bitter issue after Francis's death, splitting the order into Conventuals and Spirituals and later Observants and Capuchins, and drawing in the papacy. The rule is still professed by Franciscan friars.

title: Summa Theologiae
creator: aquinas
note: Aquinas's comprehensive synthesis of Christian theology, organised in questions and articles, the masterpiece of scholasticism.
description: Aquinas intended the Summa as a guide for beginners in theology. Its three parts treat God and creation; the human being's movement toward God through action, law, virtue and grace; and Christ and the sacraments, as the way to God. It is divided into some 500 questions and about 2,600 articles, each following a fixed method: a question, objections, an authority 'on the contrary', Aquinas's own answer and replies to each objection. It includes the 'five ways' of arguing for God's existence and an influential treatment of natural law. Aquinas stopped writing in December 1273, leaving the third part unfinished; his assistants completed it from his earlier writings. After the Council of Trent it replaced Peter Lombard's Sentences as the main textbook of Catholic theology, and it remains central to Catholic thought and widely studied by philosophers.
image_caption: An early copy of the Summa Theologiae

title: Summa contra Gentiles
creator: aquinas
location: Paris and Orvieto; autograph manuscript in the Vatican Library
note: A four-book defence of Christian truth by arguments from reason, addressed to those who do not accept scripture.
description: The Summa contra Gentiles ('against the gentiles') treats God, creation, providence and human happiness by philosophical argument in its first three books, and then truths known only by revelation, such as the Trinity and incarnation, in the fourth. A 14th-century tradition says it was written at the request of the Dominican Raymond of Peñafort as a manual for missionaries among Muslims and Jews in Spain; modern scholars debate this and see it more as an exposition of the wisdom of Christian faith in dialogue with Aristotle and his Arabic and Jewish commentators. Its third book's account of human happiness as the vision of God is a classic. Much of the autograph, in Aquinas's notoriously difficult handwriting, survives.

title: German Sermons
creator: eckhart
location: Erfurt, Strasbourg and Cologne; preserved in many manuscripts
note: Eckhart's vernacular sermons on detachment and the birth of God in the soul, the boldest mystical preaching of the Middle Ages.
description: Eckhart's German sermons, of which over a hundred are attributed to him, survive in notes and copies made by his hearers and followers rather than in his own edition, so their authenticity has had to be established by modern scholarship. Preached to Dominican nuns, Beguines and townspeople, they use paradox and striking images to speak of the soul's 'ground', where God is born, of 'detachment' (Abgeschiedenheit) from all created things and even from one's own will, and of a God beyond God, the silent desert of the Godhead. Some sentences were condemned by Pope John XXII in 1329, and Eckhart's followers preserved his teaching discreetly. Translated in the 19th and 20th centuries, the sermons have attracted philosophers, poets and readers interested in comparisons with Zen and Vedanta.

title: Revelations of Divine Love
creator: julian-of-norwich
location: Norwich; manuscripts in the British Library and Bibliothèque nationale de France
note: Julian's account of her sixteen visions and decades of reflection on them, the earliest surviving book in English by a woman.
description: Julian wrote a Short Text soon after her visions of May 1373 and, over some twenty years of reflection, a Long Text of eighty-six chapters. She describes seeing Christ's bleeding head and a small thing 'the quantity of an hazelnut' in her palm, which God told her is all that is made, kept in being by his love. She develops a theology of divine love that speaks of Jesus as our mother, of sin as having 'no manner of substance', and of the parable of a lord and servant explaining the fall. She records Christ's words that all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well. The Short Text survives in one manuscript and the Long Text in three later copies. Rediscovered in the 20th century, the book quoted by T. S. Eliot in Four Quartets, it is now one of the most read works of medieval spirituality.
image_file: The front page of Revelations of Divine Love (c. 1675, Serenus de Cressey).jpg
image_caption: Title page of Serenus de Cressy's first printed edition of the Revelations (1670)

title: The Imitation of Christ
creator: thomas-a-kempis
location: Mount Saint Agnes, near Zwolle; autograph of 1441 in the Royal Library, Brussels
note: A handbook of the inner spiritual life from the Devotio Moderna, the most widely read Christian book after the Bible.
description: The Imitation of Christ consists of four books of short chapters: counsel for the spiritual life, on the inner life, on inner consolation in the form of a dialogue between Christ and the disciple, and on the sacrament of the eucharist. It urges humility, detachment from the world, self-knowledge and personal devotion to Christ, often in pithy sayings, and is sceptical of learning that does not lead to holiness. It circulated anonymously and was attributed to various authors before scholarly consensus settled on Thomas à Kempis, whose autograph copy of 1441 survives. It has been translated into more languages than almost any other book, and read by figures as different as Ignatius of Loyola, John Wesley and Thomas More.
image_file: Thomas à Kempis - De Imitatione Christi.gif
image_caption: An early edition of De Imitatione Christi

title: Golden Legend (Legenda aurea)
creator: jacobus-de-voragine
location: Genoa and Lombardy; some 1,000 manuscripts survive; English edition by Caxton, 1483
note: A collection of saints' lives and feasts of the church year, the most popular medieval book after the Bible and a key source for religious art.
description: Organised by the liturgical calendar from Advent onward, the Golden Legend gathers some 180 chapters on saints and feasts: the lives and martyrdoms of saints such as George and the dragon, Catherine of Alexandria and Christopher, along with explanations of feasts such as Christmas and the Assumption. Jacobus drew on earlier collections and often offered several versions of a story, with fanciful etymologies of saints' names. It was a handbook for preachers and became immensely popular, translated into most European languages and printed in many editions from the 1470s. Humanists such as Juan Luis Vives criticised its legends, and the Reformation and later Catholic critical scholarship reduced its authority. Its stories shaped the iconography of medieval and Renaissance art, providing the attributes by which saints are recognised in painting and stained glass.
image_file: Umbria, jacopo da varazze, leggenda aurea, 1290 ca. 01.jpg
image_caption: An Umbrian manuscript of the Golden Legend, c. 1290

title: Wycliffite Bible
creator: wycliffe
location: Oxford and elsewhere; some 250 manuscripts survive, many in British and American libraries
note: The first complete Bible in English, translated from the Latin Vulgate by Wycliffe's followers.
description: The Wycliffite Bible exists in two versions: an early, very literal translation of the Vulgate made around 1382, and a later, more idiomatic revision of the 1390s, associated with John Purvey, whose role scholars now question. Wycliffe's personal involvement is debated; the translation was the work of a team of Oxford scholars inspired by his teaching that scripture should be available to all. In 1409 the Constitutions of Oxford, under Archbishop Arundel, forbade translating or owning the Bible in English without episcopal approval, and Lollards were prosecuted. Nevertheless, some 250 manuscripts survive, more than of any other medieval English text, many apparently owned by orthodox readers. It was a forerunner of the Reformation Bibles.
image_caption: The opening of John's Gospel in a Wycliffite Bible manuscript

title: Gutenberg Bible
creator: gutenberg
location: Copies in the Library of Congress, British Library, Bibliothèque nationale de France, Mainz Gutenberg Museum and elsewhere
note: The first major book printed in Europe with movable metal type: a two-volume Latin Vulgate of 42 lines per page.
description: Gutenberg's workshop in Mainz printed some 180 copies of the Latin Bible, about three-quarters on paper and the rest on vellum, in two large volumes of 1,286 pages, with two columns of usually 42 lines, in a Gothic type imitating the formal script of manuscripts. Production took several years and involved about 300 type designs. A letter by Enea Silvio Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II, reports seeing sheets at Frankfurt in 1454, and the books were finished by 1455. Initials, rubrics and borders were added by hand after printing, so every copy is different. Forty-nine copies, complete or substantial, survive. The Bible demonstrated that printing could match the beauty of the finest manuscripts and opened the age of the printed book, which would transform the spread of religious ideas.
image_file: Gutenberg Bible, Lenox Copy, New York Public Library, 2009. Pic 01.jpg
image_caption: The Lenox copy of the Gutenberg Bible, New York Public Library

title: Novum Instrumentum omne (Greek New Testament)
creator: erasmus
note: The first published printed Greek New Testament, with Erasmus's new Latin translation, basis of the Reformation Bibles.
description: Erasmus prepared his edition hastily from a handful of late Greek manuscripts available in Basel, printing the Greek beside his own fresh Latin translation, which departed from the Vulgate, with extensive annotations. For the end of Revelation, missing in his only manuscript, he translated the Latin back into Greek. Published by Froben in March 1516, it beat to publication the Complutensian Polyglot, printed earlier in Spain but released only in 1522. Revised editions followed in 1519, 1522, 1527 and 1535; the third added the 'Johannine Comma' on the Trinity (1 John 5:7) under pressure from critics, after a manuscript containing it was produced. Luther used the second edition for his German New Testament, and Tyndale used it for his English one. Its text, refined by later editors, became the Textus Receptus underlying the King James Version.
image_caption: Title page of Erasmus's Novum Instrumentum, Basel, 1516

title: Enchiridion militis Christiani (Handbook of the Christian Soldier)
creator: erasmus
note: Erasmus's guide to an inward, scripture-based Christian life, a manifesto of humanist piety.
description: Written, according to Erasmus, for the wife of a soldier who wanted her husband to reform his life, the Enchiridion (meaning both 'handbook' and 'dagger') sets out rules for the Christian life as a spiritual combat. It urges readers to study scripture and the Church Fathers, to seek the spirit rather than the letter, and to value inner devotion and love of neighbour above external ceremonies, pilgrimages and relics. Little noticed at first, it became a bestseller after its 1518 reissue, translated into many languages, and was read as a call for reform. It was later listed on the Spanish and Roman indexes of prohibited books, illustrating the shifting fortunes of Erasmian piety.
image_file: Erasmo de Róterdam (1528) Manual del caballero cristiano.png
image_caption: Title page of a Spanish translation of the Enchiridion, 1528

title: Ninety-five Theses
creator: luther
location: Wittenberg; printed in Nuremberg, Leipzig and Basel, 1517
note: Luther's propositions against the sale of indulgences, which set off the Protestant Reformation.
description: On 31 October 1517 Luther sent a letter to Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz protesting the preaching of indulgences by the Dominican Johann Tetzel, enclosing ninety-five Latin theses for academic debate. The famous story that he nailed them to the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg comes from Melanchthon after Luther's death; historians debate whether it happened, though posting theses on the church door was a normal way of announcing a disputation. The theses questioned the pope's power over purgatory and the value of indulgences, insisting that the true treasure of the church is the gospel. Printed and translated into German, they spread across Germany within weeks. The ensuing controversy led to Luther's excommunication in 1521. 31 October is commemorated as Reformation Day, and the 500th anniversary in 2017 was marked jointly by Lutherans and Catholics.
image_caption: An early printing of the Ninety-five Theses

title: On the Freedom of a Christian
creator: luther
note: Luther's short treatise on faith and love: a Christian is free lord of all, subject to none, and dutiful servant of all.
description: One of three great reform treatises of 1520, together with the Address to the Christian Nobility and The Babylonian Captivity of the Church, On the Freedom of a Christian was sent with a conciliatory letter to Pope Leo X. Its paradox is that faith alone, not works, justifies the Christian and unites the soul to Christ like a bride to her bridegroom, making the believer free, while that same faith overflows in love and service of the neighbour. It is the most accessible statement of Luther's understanding of justification and Christian liberty, and is still widely read.
image_caption: Title page of an early printing of Von der Freiheit eines Christenmenschen

title: Luther Bible
creator: luther
location: Printed by Hans Lufft, Wittenberg; illustrated with woodcuts from the Cranach workshop
note: Luther's German translation of the Bible from Hebrew and Greek, which shaped the German language and Protestant piety.
description: Hidden at the Wartburg castle after the Diet of Worms, Luther translated the New Testament from Erasmus's Greek text in about eleven weeks; the 'September Testament' appeared in 1522, with woodcuts from Lucas Cranach's workshop. With Melanchthon and other colleagues he then translated the Old Testament from Hebrew, and the complete Bible was published by Hans Lufft in 1534. Luther sought vivid, everyday German, famously saying that one should look at 'the mouth' of the mother in the home and the man in the market. His prefaces and some choices, such as adding 'alone' to Romans 3:28, expressed his theology. Hundreds of thousands of copies were sold in his lifetime, and the Luther Bible became a foundation of modern standard German. Revised editions are still used by German Protestants.
image_caption: Title page of the Luther Bible

title: Small Catechism
creator: luther
note: Luther's brief explanation of the Ten Commandments, Creed, Lord's Prayer and sacraments for families and children.
description: Shocked by the ignorance he found visiting Saxon parishes in 1528, Luther wrote two catechisms: the Large Catechism for pastors and the Small Catechism for heads of households to teach their families. In simple question-and-answer form, with the recurring question 'What does this mean?', it explains the Commandments, the Apostles' Creed, the Lord's Prayer, baptism, confession and the Lord's Supper, and adds prayers for morning, evening and meals. It became part of the Lutheran confessional writings in the Book of Concord (1580) and has been memorised by generations of Lutherans, one of the most widely printed books of the Reformation.
image_caption: Luther's Small Catechism, edition of 1535

title: A Mighty Fortress Is Our God (Ein feste Burg)
creator: luther
location: Wittenberg; earliest surviving printing in a 1531 hymnal
note: Luther's best-known hymn, a paraphrase of Psalm 46, often called the battle hymn of the Reformation.
description: Luther wrote some three dozen hymns, believing that congregations should sing in their own language. 'Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott' paraphrases Psalm 46 and expresses confidence in God against the devil and all earthly powers. Its exact date is uncertain, though it was probably written between 1527 and 1529; the melody, also by Luther, was originally rhythmic and lively. It became a symbol of Protestantism, used by Bach in a cantata, by Mendelssohn in his Reformation Symphony and by Meyerbeer in an opera, and has been translated into many languages, including Thomas Carlyle's English version and Frederic Hedge's 'A mighty fortress is our God'.
image_caption: Ein feste Burg in a manuscript associated with Johann Walter

title: Augsburg Confession
creator: melanchthon
location: Presented at the Diet of Augsburg, 25 June 1530
note: The primary confession of the Lutheran churches, presented to Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Augsburg.
description: When Charles V summoned the Diet of Augsburg in 1530 to settle the religious question, the Lutheran princes and cities presented a statement of their faith drafted by Melanchthon, Luther being under imperial ban and remaining at Coburg. Its twenty-eight articles set out Lutheran teaching on God, sin, justification by faith, the church and sacraments, emphasising continuity with the Catholic tradition, and then describe abuses that had been corrected, such as communion in one kind and compulsory clerical celibacy. It was read aloud in German before the emperor on 25 June. The Catholic theologians replied with a Confutation, to which Melanchthon answered with his Apology. The Augsburg Confession remains the defining statement of Lutheran churches worldwide.

title: Loci communes
creator: melanchthon
note: The first systematic presentation of Protestant theology, organised by key topics drawn from Paul's Letter to the Romans.
description: Loci communes rerum theologicarum ('common places of theology') grew out of Melanchthon's lectures on Romans. Rather than following the scholastic order, it focuses on the topics he saw as central to scripture, sin, law and grace, insisting that to know Christ is to know his benefits rather than to speculate about his natures. Luther praised it as worthy of being included in the canon. Melanchthon revised and expanded it many times until 1559, moving toward a fuller system and modifying some positions, for example on free will. It became the model for Protestant dogmatics.

title: Tyndale New Testament
creator: tyndale
location: Printed by Peter Schöffer, Worms; copies in the British Library and Stuttgart
note: The first printed English New Testament, translated from the Greek, smuggled into England and burned by the authorities.
description: Tyndale's first attempt to print his New Testament in Cologne in 1525 was interrupted by a raid, and only a fragment of that edition survives. The first complete edition was printed in Worms in 1526 in a small octavo format, and about 3,000 copies were smuggled into England, where Bishop Cuthbert Tunstall bought and burned copies at St Paul's Cross. Only three copies of the 1526 edition are known today. Tyndale went on to translate the Pentateuch (1530), Jonah and a revised New Testament (1534). His clear and rhythmic English, with phrases such as 'the salt of the earth' and 'fight the good fight', passed largely into the Great Bible, the Geneva Bible and the King James Version.
image_caption: The opening of John's Gospel in Tyndale's New Testament

title: Institutes of the Christian Religion
creator: calvin
location: First edition printed in Basel, 1536; final Latin edition Geneva, 1559
note: Calvin's systematic summary of Reformed theology, expanded from a small catechism to a monumental four-book work.
description: The first edition, of six chapters, was published in Basel in 1536 with a dedicatory letter to King Francis I of France defending persecuted French Protestants. Calvin expanded it repeatedly, and the final Latin edition of 1559, with a French translation in 1560 that helped shape French prose, is organised in four books following the Apostles' Creed: the knowledge of God the Creator; the knowledge of God the Redeemer in Christ; the way we receive the grace of Christ, including justification, the Christian life and predestination; and the church, sacraments and civil government. It opens with the claim that nearly all wisdom consists of knowing God and ourselves. The Institutes became the principal theological textbook of Reformed churches in Europe and North America.
image_caption: Title page of an edition of Calvin's Institutio

title: Genevan Psalter
creator: calvin
note: The complete book of metrical psalms in French, compiled under Calvin's direction, the songbook of Reformed Protestantism.
description: Calvin believed that congregations should sing chiefly the Psalms, in the vernacular and in unison. Beginning with a small collection in Strasbourg in 1539, he worked with the poets Clément Marot and Théodore de Bèze, who versified the psalms in French, and with musicians such as Louis Bourgeois, who composed or adapted many of the melodies, to produce the complete Genevan Psalter of 1562. Printed in tens of thousands of copies, it was translated into Dutch, German, English and other languages and remains in use in Reformed churches. The melody now known as the 'Old Hundredth', sung in English to 'All people that on earth do dwell', comes from it.
image_caption: Title page of the first Strasbourg psalter of 1539

title: Book of Common Prayer
creator: cranmer
location: London; first printed by Edward Whitchurch and Richard Grafton, 1549
note: The English prayer book that set the worship of the Church of England in Cranmer's English prose.
description: Under Edward VI, Cranmer replaced the various Latin service books of medieval England with a single book in English, combining services for morning and evening prayer, holy communion, baptism, marriage, burial and the church year, with a lectionary covering the Bible and the Psalter. The first Book of Common Prayer (1549) was conservative; the second (1552) was more firmly Protestant. Abolished under Mary I and restored under Elizabeth, it was revised in 1662, the version that remains a standard of the Church of England. Cranmer translated and adapted prayers from Latin sources and wrote new ones, in a cadenced English that gave the language phrases such as 'till death us do part' and 'ashes to ashes, dust to dust'. Versions of the prayer book shaped Anglican worship throughout the world.
image_caption: The first Book of Common Prayer, 1549

title: Spiritual Exercises
creator: ignatius-of-loyola
location: Manresa and Rome; first printed Rome, 1548
note: Ignatius's handbook for a month-long retreat of meditation and discernment, the foundation of Jesuit spirituality.
description: The Spiritual Exercises is not a book to be read straight through but a manual for a director guiding someone through a retreat, usually of about thirty days, divided into four 'weeks'. The first focuses on sin and God's mercy; the second on the life of Christ, with the famous meditations on the Two Standards and the call of the King; the third on the Passion; and the fourth on the resurrection, ending with the 'Contemplation to Attain Love'. It teaches methods of prayer using the imagination to place oneself within Gospel scenes, daily examination of conscience, and rules for 'discernment of spirits' in making decisions. Ignatius drafted it at Manresa in 1522–23 and refined it for decades; Pope Paul III approved it in 1548. It formed every Jesuit and remains widely used by Catholics and others.
image_caption: The first edition of the Spiritual Exercises, Rome, 1548

title: Interior Castle (El castillo interior)
creator: teresa-of-avila
location: Toledo and Ávila; autograph in the convent of the Discalced Carmelites, Seville
note: Teresa's guide to prayer, picturing the soul as a crystal castle of seven dwelling places with God at the centre.
description: Written in 1577 at the request of her superiors, The Interior Castle (also called The Mansions) uses the image of a castle made of a single diamond or crystal, with many rooms grouped into seven dwelling places. The soul enters through prayer and moves inward through stages of self-knowledge, struggle, the 'prayer of quiet', and the experiences of mystical union that Teresa compares to a silkworm becoming a butterfly, culminating in 'spiritual marriage' with God in the innermost room. She combines lofty experience with practical advice and humour addressed to her nuns. It is considered her masterpiece and a classic of Christian mysticism and of Spanish prose.

title: The Book of Her Life (Libro de la vida)
creator: teresa-of-avila
location: Ávila; autograph in the library of El Escorial
note: Teresa's autobiography, written for her confessors, describing her spiritual struggles, visions and the stages of prayer.
description: Teresa wrote her Life at the request of her confessors, who wanted to test the authenticity of her mystical experiences. It recounts her childhood, her entry into the Carmelites, years of illness and lukewarm prayer, and her conversion before an image of the wounded Christ. In a famous middle section she compares the stages of prayer to four ways of watering a garden, from laboriously drawing water from a well to rain falling from heaven. It also describes her vision of an angel piercing her heart with a golden spear, which Bernini sculpted in the Cornaro Chapel in Rome. The Inquisition held the manuscript for years but did not condemn it, and it was printed in 1588 in an edition by Fray Luis de León.

title: The Dark Night of the Soul
creator: john-of-the-cross
location: Composed in Granada and Andalusia; first printed in Alcalá, 1618
note: A poem of the soul's secret night journey to union with her beloved, with John's commentary on spiritual purification.
description: The poem 'En una noche oscura', 'On a dark night', in eight stanzas, tells of a woman slipping out of her quiet house at night, guided only by the light in her heart, to meet her beloved and rest with him. John wrote two prose works explaining it, The Ascent of Mount Carmel and The Dark Night, which describe the 'night of the senses' and the deeper 'night of the spirit', in which God purifies the soul by taking away consolations and certainties, leading it through apparent emptiness to union with God. The prose commentaries were left unfinished. The phrase 'dark night of the soul' has come into general use for times of spiritual desolation.

title: Spiritual Canticle
creator: john-of-the-cross
location: Begun in prison in Toledo; completed in Andalusia
note: John's lyrical dialogue between the soul and Christ, modelled on the Song of Songs, one of the great poems of the Spanish language.
description: John began the Spiritual Canticle while imprisoned in a cell in the Carmelite priory of Toledo in 1577–78, composing the first thirty-one stanzas in his head. The poem, inspired by the Song of Songs, is a dialogue in which the bride, the soul, searches for her wounded and hidden beloved through woods and meadows until they are united. He completed it later and wrote a long commentary explaining its stages of spiritual life. Two versions of the poem and commentary exist, with a different order of stanzas, and scholars debate whether the second is his revision.
image_file: Sanlucar barrameda s juan cruz manuscrito sanlucar2.jpg
image_caption: The Sanlúcar manuscript of the Spiritual Canticle

title: Introduction to the Devout Life
creator: francis-de-sales
note: A practical guide to holiness for lay people in the world, addressed to 'Philothea', a soul who loves God.
description: The Introduction grew from letters of spiritual direction Francis de Sales wrote to Madame de Charmoisy, a relative by marriage. Addressed to 'Philothea', it argues that devotion is possible and necessary for people of every condition, the soldier, the craftsman, the courtier and the married woman, not only for monks and nuns. In five parts it guides the reader from a resolution to amend her life, through prayer and the sacraments, the practice of virtues, and resisting temptations, to an annual renewal of resolutions. Its gentle, gracious style made it popular across Europe; it went through many editions in his lifetime and has been translated into many languages.

title: Decrees of the Council of Trent
creator: church-councils
note: The Catholic Church's response to the Reformation, defining doctrine on scripture, justification and the sacraments and launching wide-ranging reforms.
description: The Council of Trent met in three periods between 1545 and 1563, interrupted by war, plague and politics. In its doctrinal decrees it affirmed that revelation is transmitted through scripture and unwritten tradition, declared the Vulgate authentic, taught that justification involves both grace and human cooperation, and reaffirmed the seven sacraments, transubstantiation and the sacrificial character of the Mass. Its reform decrees required bishops to reside in their dioceses, established seminaries for training priests, and regulated religious orders, marriage and indulgences. After the council, the papacy issued the Roman Catechism (1566), a revised Missal (1570) and Breviary. Historians debate the balance of reaction and renewal at Trent, but it shaped Catholicism until the Second Vatican Council.
image_caption: A session of the Council of Trent, painting in the Castello del Buonconsiglio, Trento

title: Heidelberg Catechism
creator: church-councils
note: The catechism of the German Reformed churches, organised around guilt, grace and gratitude, still widely used.
description: Commissioned by the Elector Frederick III of the Palatinate and published in 1563, the Heidelberg Catechism was drafted mainly by the theologian Zacharias Ursinus, with Caspar Olevianus and others, though the extent of each person's contribution is debated. Its 129 questions open with 'What is your only comfort in life and death?', answered with the believer's belonging to Christ. It is organised in three parts: human misery, deliverance through Christ, and gratitude, expressed in the Ten Commandments and the Lord's Prayer, and divided into fifty-two 'Lord's Days' for preaching through the year. Approved by the Synod of Dort, it became one of the most widely used Reformed confessions in the Netherlands, Germany, Hungary and North America.
image_caption: The first edition of the Heidelberg Catechism, 1563

title: King James Version (Authorised Version)
creator: king-james-translators
note: The English Bible translated by order of James I, the most influential book in the English language.
description: Published in 1611 by the royal printer Robert Barker, the new translation was 'appointed to be read in churches'. Its translators worked from the Hebrew and Greek, with the Bishops' Bible as their base, and drew heavily on Tyndale and the Geneva Bible; their preface explains that they sought to make a good translation better. The first edition, a large folio, contains the Old and New Testaments and the Apocrypha. Early printings contained errors, and the text was standardised in the 18th century, most fully in the Oxford edition of 1769, which is the form usually read today. Although slow to replace the Geneva Bible, it became the Bible of English-speaking Protestants for three centuries, and its language profoundly influenced English literature, oratory and everyday speech, from 'the skin of my teeth' to 'a law unto themselves'.
image_caption: Title page of the first edition, 1611

title: Westminster Confession of Faith
creator: church-councils
note: The Reformed confession drawn up by the Westminster Assembly, standard of Presbyterian churches worldwide.
description: During the English Civil War, Parliament called an assembly of divines to Westminster Abbey in 1643 to reform the Church of England, with Scottish commissioners taking part. Its Confession of Faith, completed in 1646, sets out a classic Calvinist theology in thirty-three chapters, on scripture, God's decree and predestination, the covenants of works and grace, justification, the church, sacraments and civil government. The assembly also produced the Larger and Shorter Catechisms, the latter opening with the question 'What is the chief end of man?'. Adopted by the Church of Scotland in 1647, the Confession became the doctrinal standard of Presbyterian churches in Britain, America and beyond, and in modified form of some Congregational and Baptist churches.
image_file: Westminster Confession of Faith title page.jpg
image_caption: Title page of the Westminster Confession of Faith

title: Pensées
creator: pascal
location: Paris; original manuscript fragments in the Bibliothèque nationale de France
note: Pascal's unfinished notes for a defence of Christianity, including the wager and the reflections on the 'thinking reed'.
description: At his death Pascal left almost a thousand notes, some a few words, some several pages, for an apology for the Christian religion. His friends at Port-Royal published a selection in 1670, and the order of the fragments has been debated by editors ever since. Pascal describes the human condition as a mix of greatness and wretchedness, the human being as 'a reed, the feeblest thing in nature, but a thinking reed', and the restless diversions by which people avoid thinking of death. The famous wager argues that, since reason cannot decide whether God exists, one should bet on God, for if he exists the gain is infinite. Other fragments contrast the 'esprit de géométrie' with the 'esprit de finesse', and declare that 'the heart has its reasons which reason does not know'. The Pensées are a classic of French literature and of religious thought.
image_caption: An edition of the Pensées published by Guillaume Desprez, 1670

title: Provincial Letters
creator: pascal
note: Eighteen witty anonymous letters defending the Jansenists and satirising the casuistry of some Jesuit moral theologians.
description: When the Sorbonne moved to censure the Jansenist theologian Antoine Arnauld in 1656, Pascal wrote, under the pseudonym Louis de Montalte, a series of letters supposedly from a provincial gentleman to a friend. The early letters mock the disputes over grace; later ones turn to Jesuit casuists, quoting their manuals to show how they excused lying, duelling and usury through subtle distinctions. The letters were immensely popular and placed on the Index of Forbidden Books in 1657. They are regarded as a founding masterpiece of modern French prose. Historians note that Pascal's selections were sometimes unfair to the Jesuits' intentions, but the work made 'casuistry' a byword.
image_caption: An early edition of Les Provinciales
